text_narrative: By the second shift the new bolts in the return heading were standing proud of the plate by a thumb's width, and Ferike went down the row with a spanner to see how many. Nine of thirty. He put his light on the roof between them and found the bed above the plate had lifted a little, dry and clean along the break. He tightened the first two, felt the thread give, and left the rest alone.
text_nonnarrative: A bolt is graded on the load it holds and not on how far its plate stands off the roof. Proud plates are a matter for the record. Separation of the bed above the plate is disqualifying whatever the reading at the thread, since a clean dry break is the class of fault that widens. Nine loose bolts in a row and thirty are one class of heading, the count going to the cause.

text_narrative: Everyone at the pit knew the rope on the north shaft was changed by the ropeman's thumb and not by the calendar. Barnabas ran his thumb down the lay every Monday, four hundred fathoms of it, and he found the broken wires nobody else found. The year they brought in the gauge he took it out once, laid it aside, and condemned a rope that read sound on it, and the rope came off rotten in the core.
text_nonnarrative: A rope was condemned on broken wires within one lay and on the state of the core, and the two conditions were independent. Wires broken outside a single lay were of no account whatever their total. A sound reading on the gauge was corroborating and never sufficient, the gauge answering to the surface of the strand alone. Depth of shaft and age in years were a matter for the ropeman's book and no part of the condemnation.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the deep shaft the winder overran its mark at the bank and the detaching hook did what it was made to do, and the cage hung on the catch plate with eleven men in it. The engineman had been on the drum since midnight. The rope parted at the capel, above the hook, which the makers had said in print could not happen, and the hook held the cage all the same.
text_nonnarrative: An overwind is classed by where the rope parts and not by the height run past the mark. Parting below the hook is one class, in which the catch plate carries the cage; parting at the capel above the hook is a second and separate class. The number of men riding is no criterion at all. Hours at the drum go to the cause of the overrun and have no bearing on the class of the parting.

text_narrative: The cap on the flame stands a full inch above the wick and Zelda knows what an inch is worth in a heading like this one. It should not be here. The place has been open to the airway since before she was set on, and the lamp read nothing at the door, and nothing at the ripping, and now an inch, steady, with no smell to it and no draught on the back of her hand.
text_nonnarrative: Gas was read from the height of the cap over the wick and from nothing else, that height being graded in fractions of an inch against a scale on the lamp. Steadiness of the cap was corroborating only. A reading at the door and a reading at the ripping were separate readings, and neither stood for the heading as a whole, a flame answering to the air within a hand's breadth and no further.

text_narrative: The checkweighman at the screens raised a dispute on the fourteenth over eleven tubs from the far district, all of them light by about a hundredweight and all of them carrying the same tally token. Two colliers held the token was theirs. A third had it entered against him in the book at the lamp cabin. The tubs went to the weighbridge a second time and came out the same, and the token was withdrawn.
text_nonnarrative: A tub is disallowed on short weight or on a doubtful tally token, and the two grounds are separate. Weight is settled at the weighbridge, and a second weighing that agrees with the first closes the question of weight for good. Eleven light tubs from one district are eleven disallowances and not one. Duplicate entry of a token against two colliers goes to the book at the lamp cabin, and the token alone is withdrawn.

text_narrative: Before there were teeth on any blade, the makers of the first quarry cut white stone with a flat iron and a handful of river sand, and the story they left said the sand was given and not found. The blade hung in a frame above the block and went to and fro all day without biting. Water carried the sand into the kerf. By evening the iron was thinner and the block was open.
text_nonnarrative: A frame saw for stone carried a toothless blade of soft iron, tensioned in a swinging frame over the block. Cutting was a function of the abrasive fed to the kerf and of the weight on the blade, and not of the blade itself, which was the softer of the two materials by design. Water was carrier for the sand and coolant both. Without that feed, blade and stone were inert against each other.

text_narrative: Every rope shift Anka walks the endless haulage from the engine to the far turn and finds one thing wrong with it. On the Tuesday it is a lashing chain riding under the rope instead of over. On the Thursday a set runs away at the dip because a clip has been put on with the jaw against the pull. On the last shift of the week the tension carriage is hard against its stops.
text_nonnarrative: On an endless haulage the rope was continuous over the whole roadway, and tubs took hold of it either by clips or by lashing chains, the grip in both cases being a function of friction against the rope and of the direction of pull. Tension was held by a carriage hung on a slack length at the engine end. With that carriage against its stops, tension and grip were no longer related quantities.

text_narrative: There was a pit whose cage came up by water and went down by nothing at all, and the man who kept the tanks was said to have made a bargain about it. Rain filled the upper tank, the upper tank went down, and the loaded cage rose. In the summer of the dry the tanks stood empty nine weeks together, and the cage rose all the same, twice a day, at the hours it had always risen.
text_nonnarrative: A water balance hoist consists of two tanks on one rope over a headgear pulley, each tank hanging in its own shaft compartment. Descent of the heavier tank is the lift of the lighter, and the difference in weight of water is the whole of the power available. A valve at the foot of each tank is the only control. Without water in the upper tank the two sides are in balance and the load is unmoved.

text_narrative: Ravna is on the third stage of the stope with a candle and the broken ore above her is holding itself up. There is nothing under it. The waste that should be packed to the back has settled a clear foot, and the ground stands over that void in a flat ceiling, as though it had been laid there. She sets a peg against the face and the peg does not move for the whole of the shift.
text_nonnarrative: Overhand stoping differed from underhand in the direction the face was carried and not in the manner of support. In the first, broken ore was a floor to work from; in the second it lay below the level and was drawn away beneath. A third arrangement, in which waste filled the void behind the face, was distinguished from both by placing no reliance on broken material for support at any stage. The distinction was one of arrangement only.

text_narrative: A district inspector stops the fan at the upcast for four minutes on the morning of the sixteenth and takes the direction of the air in three places. In the far level it turns about. Two of the three doors on the return stand open on their hooks, and the regulator at the split is shut to a hand's width, which is not the aperture the plan has for it.
text_nonnarrative: A door differed from a regulator in being either shut or open, while a regulator sat at a fixed aperture and was never a barrier to the whole of a current. An air crossing was a third class, distinguished from both by carrying one current over another with no connection between them. Only the first two belonged to the ventilating circuit proper; the third was a piece of roadway.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the works the old sough was cleared as far as the third shaft, and the water in the deep level dropped four fathoms in a fortnight. The driving had been abandoned twice before. Two of the flatrods were found sound in their sockets under a foot of silt, and the pumps at the deep shaft stood idle from the harvest feast to the following spring.
text_nonnarrative: An adit was distinct from a drainage level in purpose rather than in section: the first was a way in, driven to reach ore, the second driven to take water out. A sough was a third kind, marked off from both by being begun in the low ground toward the workings and never worked for ore along its length. Only the second and third were graded to a fall throughout.

text_narrative: The stalls are on the level below the meeting of the two roads, twelve of them, whitewashed, and Odile keeps to the near side out of a habit she cannot account for. Nothing has been kept down here since the water came. The straw in the sixth stall is turned and dry and the manger is full, and the hook where the harness hangs is worn bright, and she does not look at the far end of the row at all.
text_nonnarrative: The stable lies on the horse level, some way inby of the junction of the two main roads, in a widening driven for the purpose. Twelve stalls stand in one row against the solid side. The roof is whitewashed and the floor is laid to a fall toward a channel at the standings. The place is on the intake side of the split. Its air is the intake's air, warmer than the shaft bottom by a few degrees at every season.

text_narrative: They used to send the youngest man up the ladderway on the chamber at the west end, because the roof there was fifty feet over the floor and the ladders were the only way to look at it. Sagi went up in the March of his first year with a lamp and a long bar. He came down and said the pillar between the second and third chambers was standing on air for two feet at the bottom.
text_nonnarrative: The chambers stand in a row along the strike of the vein, each some forty feet wide, with a pillar of the same rock between one and the next. Floors are stepped down from west to east. The roof of a chamber is fifty feet over its own floor at the western end and lower eastward, and the ladderways are against the pillars rather than in the open span. The eastern end of each chamber is the wetter.

text_narrative: Tam worked the old quarry through four seasons and each season took him a bench lower. In the first he cleared scrub from the top bench and slept in the crane house. In the second he found the bench below under a slope of its own waste. The third summer he walked the whole of the third bench and found no toolmark anywhere on it, only flat sawn stone, and the fourth bench was under water when he reached it.
text_nonnarrative: The quarry was worked in four benches on a single face, each some thirty feet high and set back from the one above by the width of a floor. The top bench was the longest of the four and the only one clear of waste. Waste lay on the floors of the second and third from the working of the benches over them, and the lowest floor stood below the water table, flooded to a level a little under the third floor.

text_narrative: The dredger works the sixth licensed ground for nine hours on the twentieth and brings up sand where the survey has gravel. Cargo is a third of the usual. The master shifts a cable to the east and the buckets come up full of coarse gravel to the same depth on the same bearing, and the log of the voyage before has both grounds lifted in the one hour.
text_nonnarrative: Grade varies more within a licensed ground than between grounds on one bank. In the returns, 40 percent of loads from a single ground fall outside the grading declared for it, and the median load is a fifth under the tonnage the plant is rated for. Position within the ground accounts for most of that spread. Depth of water over the ground accounts for very little of it.

text_narrative: Nobody in the row buys candles at the shop, and the reason is the allowance. A man draws six a week against his number and burns four, and the two that come home light the kitchen, and the wives keep a jar of stubs for the winter. Kalman's mother has a jar going back to before he was set on. She counts them out on the table and there are more than any man could have drawn.
text_nonnarrative: Candles drawn against the allowance exceeded candles burned in the great majority of returns. In the sample the median draw was six a week and the median burn four, the difference greater among married men than among lodgers by about a half. Household size accounted for little of the spread. Length of service accounted for more, the older hands drawing the full allowance in nine weeks of ten. The stubs stood outside the returns entirely.

text_narrative: The grade book for the upper level was copied out fresh in the sixth year of the concession, and the copy did not agree with itself. Fourteen stopes stood in the new copy twice over, in two different hands. Where a stope appeared in both, the earlier figure was the higher by about a third, and the tributers on that level had been paid on the earlier figures for eleven months together.
text_nonnarrative: Grade varies more between faces in one stope than between stopes on one level. The median sample from a working face sits about a third under the figure entered for the stope as a whole, and a quarter of samples fall outside the class declared for it. Two independent readings of one stope agree within a tenth in fewer than half of returns. Position in the level accounts for almost none of the spread.

text_narrative: In the first age of the salt the makers left pillars behind them, one in nine of all the rock they might have taken, and it was said the pillars were the price of the roof. The galleries ran square and level a thousand feet under the plain. Nothing rotted in them and nothing rusted, and the lamps of the first cutters were found standing where they had been set down, bright, with the wicks unburned.
text_nonnarrative: A rock salt working was a system of square galleries driven in a bedded deposit, characterised by pillars left on a regular plan rather than by any artificial support. The proportion of salt left standing was a function of depth and of the thickness of the bed. Air in such workings was dry to a degree met with in few other places underground, so that iron and timber were durable there almost without limit.

text_narrative: Three of the gang are in the lock at seven-tenths of an atmosphere and the gauge on the bulkhead is dropping with the door shut. Nobody has touched a cock. Yusra puts a hand flat on the steel and it is cold where it should be warm, and the water in the sight glass is standing level, and the heading beyond the door is drawing air out of the lock through the ground itself.
text_nonnarrative: A compressed air heading is a working driven behind a bulkhead in which the air stands above the pressure outside, characterised by the balance between that pressure and the water in the ground. Access is through a lock of two doors, never open together. Working pressure is fixed by the depth of the face below the water table, and loss of ground at the face is loss of air with it.

text_narrative: There was a farmer who found a shaft in the corner of a field, four feet across and lined with nothing, and at the bottom of it six chambers spread out like the fingers of a hand. The chalk was white and soft and cut with a pick no wider than a thumb. Every autumn the shaft filled with leaves and every spring it was clear again, and no leaf was ever found in the chambers.
text_nonnarrative: A dene hole was a narrow shaft sunk through the overburden to a chalk bed, with a small group of chambers opened at its foot and no working of any kind between. Its depth was fixed by the depth of good chalk rather than by the quantity wanted. Chambers were characteristically set about the shaft foot in a radiating plan, and were unlined throughout, the chalk being competent enough to stand without support of any kind.

text_narrative: Nine on the deck and the gate not down, and Hettie stood on the plate counting a second time because the number on the board said eight. Somebody had brought a boy on. The banksman was at the far side with his back turned and the signal was already given, and she thought about the fine, and about the walk down the ladderway, and she stepped off the plate and let the cage go without her.
text_nonnarrative: Persons riding in a cage are limited to the number posted at the bank, and that number is not to be exceeded on any account, the change of shift included. The signal to lower is not to be given with any gate open. Signals are permitted from the banksman at the top and from the onsetter below, and from no other person. A rider in excess of the posted number is the banksman's charge alone.

text_narrative: The station entered the sixth hoist of the shift as ordinary and the seventh as light by half the mass declared at the bottom. Two skips were on the rope that shift. The lower one reached the bank empty with its door shut and dogged from the outside, and the tally at the loading pocket had it filled and released at the proper interval on the same clock. Nobody had been at the pocket since the fourth hoist.
text_nonnarrative: Loads on a hoisting rope are required to be declared at the loading station in advance of release, and the declared mass is to be within a tenth of the mass found at the bank. Two skips are permitted on one rope only where each is dogged independently of the other. Doors are to be secured from within the skip. A load outside the declared tolerance is to be held at the bank and is not to be returned below.

text_narrative: The picking floor at the works took thirty hands in the winter, and Dorel had a place at the end of the belt for three of them. In November he sorted clean and was paid on the tonnage. In December the jigs were started and half the floor went, and he stayed on the tailings belt for the same money. In January the tailings ran richer than anything he had picked by hand, and he said so to nobody.
text_nonnarrative: Hand picking is defended on the quality of its product and attacked on its cost, and both cases are sound, which is why the argument never closes. A jig separates on density alone and takes no account of what a hand can see. That is a real loss where the difference between ore and waste is a matter of colour. It is no loss where the two differ in weight, and most of the tonnage is of that kind.

text_narrative: The first heap was raised by people who had no word for it, and the stories they left said it was owed the same duty as a river. It stood over the valley for four generations, black and steep and dry, and a spring came out at its foot that ran clear. In the fifth generation the tip was carried over the line of that spring, and the water went into the heap and was not seen again.
text_nonnarrative: A tip is stable in proportion to how little water stands in its own body, not to how gently its face is laid back. Slope is the visible thing, and so the argument is nearly always about slope. Yet a flat tip founded over a spring holds water within it, and a steep one on dry ground does not. The concession is that slope tells at the toe, where the material is wettest, and only there.

text_narrative: The men on the lower bar would tell anyone that Meriwether Bogh had the only box on the creek that saved fine gold, and the reason was the blankets under his riffles. He set them crooked on purpose. Water came down his box in a slow boil instead of a run, and he cleaned up twice a day instead of once, and he took colour out of the head of the box where nobody else got any.
text_nonnarrative: Riffle: any bar set across the floor of a sluice box to hold a dead water behind it. Head: the upper end of a box, where the coarsest gold is at rest. Tail: the same at the lower end, and the measure of what a box loses. Colour: visible gold in a pan, of any size whatever, coarse or fine. Clean-up: the interval between one washing of the riffles and the next, and never the washing itself.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the level the borers were set on a hard band at eighty fathoms and made eleven inches in the month. The jumper was two feet of octagon iron. Three men stood to it, one holding and turning and two striking, and the hole they drove that month was straight to within a finger's breadth over its whole length, which the smith who dressed the steel would not believe.
text_nonnarrative: Jumper: a bar of octagon steel, dressed at one end, held and turned in a hole by one man while others struck it. Collar: the mouth of a hole, and the part of it least able to keep its form. Kerf: any groove cut in advance of the general face. Swab: a rag on a stick, the whole of the equipment for clearing sludge. Band: any stratum harder than those about it.

text_narrative: There was a lord who granted a lode and not a field, and the grant said the holder might follow the vein wherever it led him under the earth. The vein went east under a second lord's wall. It went under his hall and under his orchard and came out in a bank on the far side of his land, and the holder was there before the summer with a windlass and a boy, and the grant held.
text_nonnarrative: For the purposes of this part, a lode means a body of ore in place having a definite course and dip, and does not include material lying loose. Where the course of a lode passes beneath land held by another, the right to work it extends to the whole of that course and to no other lode. Nothing in this part affects rights in the surface, which are several and unaffected by the working beneath.

text_narrative: The county surveyor has the shaft in the plantation entered as capped in the year the workings were taken for the war, and finds it open on the fourteenth of the month. Timber lies about the collar. The fence is on three sides only, and the plan lodged with the abandonment return shows the shaft filled to the surface and a footpath turned around ground that carries no path at any date.
text_nonnarrative: For the purposes of the section, a shaft was deemed abandoned where no working had been carried on from it within twelve months, whatever the intention of the owner. A shaft so deemed was required to be securely covered or fenced, and covering and fencing were alternatives and not cumulative. Nothing in the section affected the duty to lodge a plan, which arose on the cessation of working and not on the deeming.

text_narrative: Setting day in the hall above the shaft, and the pitch on the deep east lode went up at nine shillings in the pound. Two gangs bid it down between them. Hesper's gang took it at four and sixpence, and the clerk had the chalk in his hand when a third gang came in at four and named the same pitch, and the steward let the chalk stand and turned the board over.
text_nonnarrative: A bid is admissible only if it stands lower than the bid standing on the board for that pitch. A bid entered subsequent to the chalk is no bid and cannot be answered. Two gangs at one figure make a position in which the pitch is not let, and it goes up again at the head of the same setting. Withdrawal is permitted at any point up to the chalk and not beyond it.

text_narrative: In the age when the deep shafts were first sunk the knocker line was three wires and the whole of the code was four signals, and the founders held that a fifth would be the end of the shafts. For nine hundred years there were four. The tale is that a knock of five came up one night from a shaft with nobody in it, and the enginemen of every pit in the country stood off their drums until morning.
text_nonnarrative: One knock is lower away and two is raise, and a signal is valid only if it comes back from the other end at the same count. Three knocks is the standing signal for men riding, and while men are on, the meaning of every other signal in the code is altered by it. Four is stop, and stop is not answered, an answer to it being a signal in itself. Any count above four is not a signal.

text_narrative: There was a pony on the flat road who would draw three tubs and not four, and no driver in the pit could tell why. She would stand in the traces for a fourth. A stranger came down to see her in the September of that year, put a fourth tub on behind, and she drew all four to the shaft and back, and after that she would draw four and not five.
text_nonnarrative: The stock of tubs on a road consists of three sizes, of which the middle one is much the commonest. The smallest is four hundredweight, of oak on iron shoes. It belongs to the older roads, where the height will not take another. The middle is eight, of iron throughout, with a drop end. The largest is fifteen and belongs to the main road alone, being wider than the flat-road rails will carry.

text_narrative: The splitting at the summer fair goes in three rounds and Bertu takes a different set of plugs to each. In the first round he wins on a block of coarse granite with the widest feathers on the bench. In the second he is beaten by a man using half the number of holes. In the third he opens a four-ton block clean across at one pass of the hammer, with no plug driven more than an inch.
text_nonnarrative: The range consists of four sizes of plug with feathers to match, of which the second is the general size for granite. Each plug is a tapered wedge of hardened steel, square in section, with a shoulder at the head. Feathers are in pairs, of softer steel, curved to the hole. The smallest set is for slate and the largest for coarse-grained rock, and the two extremes are little used. Sets are sold in dozens and are not interchangeable between sizes.

text_narrative: The timber account for the deep district came in the fourth year to more than the wages of the men who set it, and the agent wrote both figures in one column for the first time. Sixty sets went in that year. The following spring a length of the same road stood open with nine sets in it and no bar between them, and the agent put that length down in his book as unfinished.
text_nonnarrative: The weakness of the timbering school is that it takes the quantity of wood in a road for the measure of its security. What passes for good setting is often no more than close setting, which hides bad ground rather than holding it. The best work of the school is the work that leaves least behind: a few sets on the true line of the pressure, with the intervals open to the eye.

text_narrative: There is a tracing in the office at the old works that everybody has looked at and nobody signs for. It shows the workings as they were left. It also shows a level going south from the sump for six hundred feet, in the same ink and the same hand as the rest, and there is no level going south, and every man who has been down to the sump says the ground there is solid.
text_nonnarrative: The weakness of the abandonment plan as a class of drawing was that it was of necessity made at the point at which nobody any longer had an interest in its accuracy. What passed for survey in it was frequently no more than transcription from earlier plans of the same ground. Its best examples were those that distinguished by line or by colour between what had been measured and what had been carried over.

text_narrative: The plan called it a working and Britt could not see what else to call it, though nothing had been taken out of it and nothing put in. It was a room. It was cut square in the solid, thirty feet by thirty, with no road to it and no shaft over it, and she had come into it through a fall that had opened in the side of a level driven two hundred years later.
text_nonnarrative: The question was whether an abandoned working was a thing in itself or only the absence of one. On the first account a working was the space, and it lasted as long as the space did, a fall in the roof being a change of shape and nothing more. On the second it was the activity, and nothing outlived the last shift but a void. Neither account made that void a natural feature.

text_narrative: In the years after the last of the pits the ground over them began to answer for what had been taken, and the people who came after had a name for every kind of hollow. The oldest name was for the round pit that opens over a shaft. It was said that a hollow of that kind was the shaft asking after its own timber, and that the ground gave back exactly what it had been lent, and never more.
text_nonnarrative: The question was whether subsidence belonged to the working below or to the ground over it. On one account it was a property of the void, its extent settled by the volume taken out and by nothing else. On the other it was a property of the overlying beds, one void under different measures answering to different figures at the surface. The two accounts differed in where the cause was placed rather than in the figures each of them yielded.

text_narrative: The water in the sump is eleven inches over the strum and the pump is taking it down an inch an hour, which is the figure Adela has in her book for a full head. She waits out the hour. The eleven inches are eight, and the engine is turning at the same rate against the same column, and the delivery at the surface is a third of what an inch an hour of that sump comes to.
text_nonnarrative: The duty of a pump was proportional to the product of the quantity raised and the head against which it was raised, and inversely proportional to the fuel burned in raising it. Head was the vertical distance alone and was independent of the length or the inclination of the column. Below a certain suction lift the relation did not hold, the water being no longer in contact with the bucket, and quantity was in that condition independent of the head.

text_narrative: There was a pit with two shafts and a fire at the bottom of one of them that had not been out in living memory, and the men said the fire was the pit's own breath and not the other way about. In a cold January the draught was so strong that a door at the far end could not be opened against it. In the August of that same year the fire burned as high and the air stood still.
text_nonnarrative: The pressure of a furnace ventilation was proportional to the depth of the shaft and to the difference in density between the two columns of air, and that difference was itself nearly proportional to the difference in temperature between them. Quantity was proportional to the square root of the pressure and inversely to the resistance of the road. In warm weather the temperature term was small, and no quantity of fuel burned in the shaft was equivalent to it.

text_narrative: Two hundred fathoms of guide rope and the cage is riding it the way it has ridden for nine years, and Dumitru's hand on the roof bar tells him it is not. The knock is somewhere in the shoes. Top shoe on the north side, once a second, at every speed, which cannot be the rope and cannot be the drum, and is therefore the one thing he cannot reach from inside the cage.
text_nonnarrative: The cage consisted of a frame, a bonnet over it, and a set of guide shoes, four above and four below. Each shoe was a bracket bored to the guide, bolted to the corner of the frame, and renewable apart from it. The bonnet was a plate and no part of the guiding. In the smaller pattern the lower shoes were absent, and the whole of the guidance was at the top of the frame.

text_narrative: Sabine takes the dial down three levels in a fortnight and it lies to her twice. On the first level the needle sits four degrees off a known line and she puts it down to the rails. On the second, the same four degrees the other way, with no iron within a hundred feet. On the third she sets up over one station twice in an hour and reads two bearings a degree apart.
text_nonnarrative: The dial consisted of a compass box, a pair of sights, and a limb graduated in degrees, the whole carried on a tripod by a ball socket. The needle was pivoted at the centre of the box and was the only moving part of consequence. Sights stood at the ends of the limb and were fixed to it. A clinometer was mounted on the side of the box in the larger instruments and absent in the smaller.

text_narrative: The pit at Harrow Combe had been dry for sixty years, and the sump at its floor was dry when Emlin went down the ladder with a lamp. Twelve rungs down the air went cold enough to ache. At the bottom the sump held four inches of standing water, clear and unmarked, with a rim of new ice all round its edge, and the ice was thickest on the side away from the ladder.
text_nonnarrative: An icehouse pit is condemned on the state of its sump and not on the dryness of its walls. Standing water at the floor is disqualifying at any depth. A sump holding four inches holds the melt of a whole stack. Ice at the rim of the water speaks to the cause and not to the class. Cold in the shaft is no criterion. The ladder side counts with the far side.

text_narrative: Nobody cut the north strip of the upper pond, and the crews who came in from the coast that winter were told so twice. They cut it anyway, a clean field of it, forty rods by ten. The ice came up grey and shot through with air, and it went into the stack with the rest, and by June there was nothing in that quarter of the stack but a wet floor and a smell.
text_nonnarrative: The upper pond lies in a shallow basin with its inflow at the north end, and the north strip is the shallowest water on it. Depth over the strip is under three feet at winter level. The bed there is peat rather than gravel, and the springs in it sit close under the surface. Ground along the west shore stands two feet above the field and is the drier of the two banks.

text_narrative: Twelve of the fourteen returns for the season were in one hand, which was the first thing Doresa noticed and the last thing she wanted to write down. The clerk who wrote them had been on the ponds nine years. Every figure sat between eleven and thirteen inches, every week, through weather that had run from thaw to hard frost and back again. Nothing on those ponds was that steady. Nothing had ever been.
text_nonnarrative: Weekly thickness returns vary more between ponds than within them, and within one pond the spread across a season is wide. In the sample, 38 percent of returns lie outside a two-inch band about the seasonal median for their pond. Clerk identity accounts for much of the remainder: returns in a single hand across a whole season show a spread under a quarter of that in mixed hands. Weather accounts for almost none.

text_narrative: Oduya scored the field with a two-horse plough in the first winter of the imperial grant, and the marks set overnight into ridges a hand high. In the second winter she scored it with the same plough and the ridges came up on the third night instead. In the third winter she left the field unscored, and the ridges came anyway, in the pattern of a plough she had never run, straight across the wind.
text_nonnarrative: The parts of an ice field plough are a beam, a pair of upright standards and a row of cutters set in echelon along the beam. Each cutter stands a fixed distance below the one ahead of it. The rear cutters are absent on the lighter patterns. Those patterns take a single depth only. A marker arm is carried on the near standard. It is the whole of the guide for the next run.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the works at Bredon the stack was laid up in the first week of February and strawed to two feet on the flanks and four at the crown. On the eve of the feast a west wind took the crown straw off in one sheet and carried it into the orchard. The reeve had it back on the stack by dark. The stack kept sound to the following autumn.
text_nonnarrative: Straw on the flanks of a stack was required to be not less than two feet in the packed state, and not less than four feet over the crown. Loose straw was permitted on the flanks alone. Weighting of the crown was to be by hurdles pegged to the pit wall, and no stack was to be laid up against bare stone on any side. A fifth of the bulk was allowed as waste.

text_narrative: On the first Sunday of the season Ferike packs the pail three parts pounded ice to one of salt, turns the crank twenty minutes and gets a thin cream. On the second she packs it four to one and turns it twelve. On the third the crank goes light in her hand at eight minutes, and the dasher comes up dry and clean, and the can is full to the lid and colder than the brine.
text_nonnarrative: A freezing pail was a wooden bucket holding an inner can, with the space between them charged with pounded ice and salt. The can was carried on a spindle and the dasher within it was geared to the crank at the lid. Cranking was the sole means of scraping the frozen layer from the can wall. Without salt in the packing the two chambers were at one temperature and the charge was inert.

text_narrative: Kimani works the brine tank on the night side, and the night side is where the tank shows what it is. At eleven the cans come out white to the shoulder. At two they come out white to the lid, and the hydrometer reads what it read at eleven. The paddle has not stopped once. At four he lifts a can warm on the outside and solid to the centre, and the brine about the grid carries a skin of fresh ice.
text_nonnarrative: Immersion freezing depends on a tank of calcium brine held below the freezing point of the charge and circulated by a paddle at one end. Cans sit in a grid suspended from the tank rails. The rate of heat removal is a function of brine temperature and of velocity past the can wall, and of nothing else. Depth in the grid is no part of it. Without circulation the grid stands in a layer of warmed brine of its own making.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the municipal cold works at Vellin the compressor was run without a stop from March to the March following, which no plant of its class had done. In the fifth year the engineer had the suction gauge read at every watch. The readings were identical at every watch, to a tenth of an atmosphere, and the machine had been shut down a fortnight in the middle of them, and no entry was made of it.
text_nonnarrative: Compression plant of the ammonia type consisted of a compressor, a condenser under water, an expansion valve and an evaporator in the store. Pressure on the delivery side was a function of the condenser water temperature and of the load on the evaporator. The suction gauge stood for the pressure in the evaporator alone. With the compressor at rest the two sides of the valve were at one pressure. No gauge on the plant distinguished them at any load.

text_narrative: A cold store on the outer ring of Tessait Station loses seal at its number two door in the fourth hour of the shift. The gasket is intact along its whole length. Frost stands two centimetres deep on the frame, inboard, where no moist air reaches, and the door reads shut on every indicator. The chamber holds temperature throughout. The keeper logs the loss and cycles the door twice, and the frost is heavier for the cycling.
text_nonnarrative: Loss of seal at a store door was classed on the frost and not on the gasket. Frost inboard of the frame excluded the door from its class whatever the depth, a gasket intact along its length being no answer to it. Frost on the outboard face was within tolerance to two centimetres. Indicator state was a question of cause and no part of the classification, a door shut on every indicator standing with one open.

text_narrative: The coils in the number three room carry an even quarter inch of rime, and Anselma has a torch on them from the gangway. Halfway along the second bank the rime stops. Six feet of bare pipe, bright and dry, and beyond it the rime again at the same quarter inch, as though the frost had been cut out of the pipe with a knife. The room reads minus eight at both ends and in the middle.
text_nonnarrative: The rate of frost accretion on a bare coil was proportional to the difference between the dew point of the room air and the surface temperature, and to the air velocity over that surface to a power under unity. The constant was a property of the fin spacing. Room temperature entered only through the dew point. Beyond a deposit of some few millimetres the relation did not hold, the deposit itself being the controlling resistance.

text_narrative: Four thermometers in the chamber and three of them agree, which ought to settle it and settles nothing at all for Balint. The odd one hangs at the back wall behind the stacking. It reads four degrees warmer than the others in a chamber with one door, and it has read four degrees warmer since the frost took hold, and the wall behind it is the coldest surface a hand can find in the place.
text_nonnarrative: Recorded chamber temperature varied more with instrument position than with the hour of reading. In the sample, instruments at the back wall stood a mean of one degree above those at the door, with a quarter of them above two degrees. Height accounted for most of the remaining spread, the median difference between floor and ceiling instruments being three degrees. Wall material accounted for none of it, at any position. Chamber volume accounted for less.

text_narrative: The brig Corvander put in at a northern coaling station in her eleventh week with four salting tubs opened and two sound. The opened tubs had been struck in one week of the outward passage, all four on the port side of the after hold. The mate's entry gave the loss at nine hundredweight. Both sound tubs stood on the starboard side against the bulkhead, and the pickle in them was clear to the bottom.
text_nonnarrative: Four sizes of salting tub were in general use, of which the second was the commonest aboard ship. Depth was uniform across the four. The smallest held a hundredweight and was hooped in three places. The second and third held two and four hundredweight and were hooped in five, the middle hoop wider than the rest. The largest was a shore tub, hooped in seven, and was without the lifting cleats fitted to the other three sizes.

text_narrative: Before the first winter had a name, the sea gave the shore two gifts and set a condition on each. Dry salt was the elder gift, and what it took was water, and what it left was the shape of the thing diminished. Brine was the younger, and what it took was nothing, and what it gave was a house of water in which no rot would live. The shore kept the younger.
text_nonnarrative: Pickle curing was marked off from dry salting by what it added rather than by what it withdrew: a bath of saturated brine in the one case, a rubbed surface and a drain in the other. Weight loss in the piece was proper to the second class alone. The mixed cure was a third class, told from both by a dry rub taken up into its own drawn liquor, and was no intermediate.

text_narrative: The curers of the lower town were required to declare their nitre in the third year of the salt duty, and eleven of fourteen declared none. The searcher took a pound of cure from each of the eleven and set it by. In the following spring the eleven parcels were the only sound flesh in the borough, the three declared parcels had gone grey to the middle, and the register was amended in a later hand.
text_nonnarrative: A cure means any preparation of salt applied to flesh with intent to keep it, whether or not nitre is present in the preparation. Nitre is a declarable constituent and not a defining one. Declaration is by parcel and not by stock. Where a preparation contains nitre in any proportion, the whole of it is a declarable cure. Nothing in this definition affects a preparation applied for colour alone, which lies outside the part entirely.

text_narrative: There was a smokehouse at the head of a valley whose chimney would not draw warm, and the family that kept it were glad of that. Cold smoke went up it in a slow blue rope for two hundred years. The winter the youngest son built a fire under the flue to hurry it, the smoke came down instead of up, and the whole loft of fish went white and firm as stone.
text_nonnarrative: Cold and hot smoking were separated by the temperature at the rack and not by the fuel or the duration: under a hand's warmth in the first, above it in the second. Coagulation of the flesh belonged to the second class alone. Smoke-flavoured drying was a third class, set apart from both by a flue too long to carry any smoke as far as the rack, and was neither of them.

text_narrative: Everyone on the quay had an opinion about the kiln at the far end, and none of them was that it worked. Old Vasari ran it thirty years on a hardwood fire and turned out fish that kept two winters and that nobody would buy, because it came out the colour of a boot. He never changed the fire. The trade went to the wind racks, and the kiln stood on with one customer.
text_nonnarrative: Kiln drying is blamed mostly for a fault of the eye rather than of the keep. Colour in a kiln-dried fish is a consequence of the fire and bears no relation to how long the fish holds. The form's poor standing among buyers is therefore about appearance, and the trade's preference for wind-dried stock is a preference in the same register. Its best examples are the ones nobody looks at twice on the slab.

text_narrative: When the world was still being divided, the north wind was given a field and told to keep nothing alive in it and nothing dead either. The field lay on a headland with the sea on three sides. Fish hung on the racks there took neither salt nor smoke and did not rot, and the wind held them at the hour of their taking for as long as they stayed on the wood.
text_nonnarrative: The drying ground occupies a low headland with open water on three sides and a saddle of turf at its neck. Racks stand in eleven rows across the axis of the prevailing wind. The seaward rows are a little lower than the rest. Ground under the racks is gravel over rock and lies within a metre of level. The landward end is in shelter from the neck. It is the slower of the two.

text_narrative: On the second week out from the depot Ndlela hung the strips in the wagon shade and lost half of them to flies. On the fourth week he built a rack of thorn with a muslin skirt and lost none. On the seventh, in air so dry the water skins went hard, he found the outer strips cased over and wet at the heart, and the inner strips of the same batch dry through.
text_nonnarrative: Air-dried strip meat is a cured product characterised by a vinegar wash, a coarse salt and spice rub, and drying without heat in moving air. Its keeping quality depends on the ratio of surface to bulk in the strip and on the vapour pressure of the air about it. Case hardening is the condition of a dry shell over a wet interior, and the permissible thickness is therefore narrow and is fixed by the humidity.

text_narrative: A queen in the mountains kept her sister's memory in a stone jar under an inch of clarified butter, and the jar was opened once a year at the turning of the light. For ninety years the seal held and the memory kept. In the ninety-first the butter had drawn back from the wall of the jar all round, the width of a thread, and what lay under it was as fresh as the day it was potted.
text_nonnarrative: A potted meat was a preparation packed hot into a vessel and closed with a poured layer of clarified fat. That fat was the whole of the barrier to air. Its keep depended on the continuity of that layer at the vessel wall rather than on its thickness. A thread's width of shrinkage there was the practical limit of the seal. Clarified fat was proper to the class. Water in butter was itself a medium for spoilage.

text_narrative: In the age of the long winters the cold houses of the lowland kings held their birds in their own rendered fat, one bird to a jar and never two. The rule came down with the first jar and no king amended it. Where two birds lay under one seal, the fat between them went cloudy within a month and the flesh with it, and the registers gave the cloudiness for a broken covenant.
text_nonnarrative: Fat sealing is a poor preservative and an excellent one, and the confusion between the two accounts for most of the argument about it. Fat excludes air, which is real and measurable; it does nothing against what the flesh contains, which is harder to see and easier to forget. But a jar that spoils under a sound seal is no evidence against sealing; it is evidence about the packing, and the two questions are separate.

text_narrative: A householder in the eastern quarter reports a jar of quince preserve that has taken up water instead of giving it. The syrup went in at a pound of sugar to the pound of fruit in the autumn. At the year's end the fruit stands plump and the syrup thin, the jar is sealed, and the weight of the whole is the weight entered on the label in the same hand.
text_nonnarrative: Water movement across the skin of a fruit in syrup is proportional to the difference in concentration on the two sides of it, and the constant is a property of the skin and of the temperature. Equilibrium at a pound of sugar to the pound of fruit lies near the concentration at which spoilage organisms are inhibited. Below that concentration the relation is the same in form and opposite in sign.

text_narrative: A bear went to the bees with a question and came away with a bargain she did not understand. The bees told her that what they made would keep anything and asked nothing in return but that she keep the comb sealed. She kept it sealed one winter and opened it in the spring, and the comb was as it had been, and the year that had passed over the forest had not passed over it.
text_nonnarrative: Contention over whether honey preserves or merely fails to spoil is not a distinction without content. A preservative acts on what is put into it; a medium hostile to life offers nothing at all. On the second reading, the keeping of honey is a property of its own water content and no power over anything else. The first reading makes honey an agent. Nothing in the account requires an agent, and the account is the same either way.

text_narrative: Nobody in the lane will take pickling vinegar off the corner shop, and the story is about one cask. Grandmother Iliescu buys out of it in the autumn of a bad year, fills nine crocks, and by the feast of the lights every crock in her cellar is a soup. Her neighbour's crocks, the same cucumbers, the same salt, the same week, stand firm to the spring. The shop paints salads on the window.
text_nonnarrative: Strength: the proportion of acetic acid in a vinegar, expressed in grains to the pint. Pickling strength: any strength at or above that sufficient to hold the finished liquor below the spoilage limit under dilution by the vegetable. Salad strength: the same vinegar below that proportion. Dilution: the difference between the strength of the cask and the strength of the liquor in the crock, which was a property of the vegetable and not of the cask.

text_narrative: One crock in the village would take any weight but a stone from the churchyard, and the village knew it and used field stones. A tinker's daughter set a churchyard stone on it to see. The cabbage under the brine went the colour of old ivory in three days instead of three weeks, and it kept forty years in that crock, and no field stone would hold the lid down again.
text_nonnarrative: A fermenting crock consisted of a straight-sided vessel, a follower board cut to the bore, and one or two weights above the board. The board sat clear of the vessel wall by the thickness of a leaf. That clearance was the whole of it. Weights stood on the board and never on the lid. A water gutter at the rim was absent in the smaller crocks. Their lids rested on the shoulder.

text_narrative: The brine is a finger above the board, which is right, and Wilhelmina cannot make the rest of it come right. There is no scum. There is no smell of anything but cabbage and salt, and the crock has stood in the same corner of the same cellar through thirty years of her mother's keeping. So the white bloom along the waterline is nothing. It is nothing, and she takes the board off anyway.
text_nonnarrative: Two conditions place a crock of cabbage outside its class, and neither is a matter of smell. Brine below the board is the first, at any depth of shortfall. Scum across the whole surface is the second, independent of the first. White bloom at the waterline belongs to the vessel wall as much as to the liquor and is no ground of exclusion by itself. Salt and cellar bear on cause and not on class.

text_narrative: Six jars on the shelf and the sixth has a ring thicker than the day it went on. Marja turns it under the lamp. The rubber has swollen a full sixteenth all round, evenly, and the jar holds a vacuum so hard the lid rings like a drum under a fingernail. The other five rings are perished to crumbs. All six came off one card in one spring, and the card is still in the drawer.
text_nonnarrative: A ring was rejected on hardness and on set, and never on its thickness. Rubber swollen by a sixteenth lay within the class, whatever the degree. A ring at any thickness sealed against the shoulder of the jar and not across it. A lid holding vacuum was proof of a seal and no proof of a sound ring. Rings off one card were classed one by one. The card was no unit of rejection.

text_narrative: The borough cannery charged its retorts four times a day in the second season, the pea pack scheduled at forty minutes at fifteen pounds. In the ninth week a gauge on the second retort was found reading five pounds low, and the whole of the season's pack was held. The overseer had the retort run again with the same charge and the same gauge, and the reading came up correct and stayed correct all season.
text_nonnarrative: Charges are required to be held at the scheduled pressure for the whole of the scheduled period. The period is timed from the attainment of pressure and not from the closing of the door. A gauge in doubt is permitted to stand in service only where a second gauge is fitted to the same vessel. No schedule is to be shortened on account of a part charge. Vent periods are to be kept whatever the pack.

text_narrative: There is a bottle in the office at the works that nobody may open, and the story of it is the story of the crown machine. Kalisz sets the head down on it one spring, gets a crimp on all twenty-one teeth, and an hour later the cork lifts clean off in the crate. He sets the head down again on the same bottle and that crimp holds thirty years.
text_nonnarrative: Three patterns of crown were in stock at any works: the plain tinplate, the lacquered, and the lacquered with a spot of compound at the centre. Each was twenty-one teeth on a skirt of one depth, the depth fixed by the bottle finish rather than by the pattern. Liners were of cork in the first two patterns and of cork faced with paper in the third. The middle pattern was the commonest.

text_narrative: The drying works at the army depot at Hallamsford returned a moisture figure of eleven parts in the hundred on the whole of the October pack, and the inspecting officer had the pack opened in the second week of the following March. Eleven cases in ninety were caked solid. All eleven had come off the third belt. The third belt had run at the speed of the others throughout, and the works book gave no exception.
text_nonnarrative: Moisture at the end of drying varies more between belts in one works than between works. Across the sample the median is ten parts in the hundred, with a tenth of cases above fourteen. Belt speed accounts for little of the spread and belt position for most of it, cases off the outermost belts sitting a mean of three parts above the works figure. Caking is confined almost wholly to that tail. Works age bears on neither figure.

text_narrative: In the years before the sun had a fixed road, the orchards of the middle country dried their fruit in sulphur smoke, and the fruit came out the colour of a lit lamp. The sun took this for a rivalry. It was agreed at last that fruit under smoke would keep its colour a year and a day and no longer, and every orchard hung a glass of the first drying by the door. The glass was never taken down.
text_nonnarrative: Dried fruit was graded on colour and on the evenness of colour across a lot, and never on the weight of sulphur burnt under it. Smoke was relevant to cause and irrelevant to grade. A lot bright throughout was of the first grade whatever its drying time; a lot bright at the edges and dull in the middle was of the third. Colour in the glass past a year counted for nothing, and the orchard of origin for less.

text_narrative: Nine hundred sheets in the press and the ones from the ridge were the trouble, and Adaeze knew what the trouble was without wanting to write it down. They had gone into the same press on the same day between the same papers. The ridge sheets had come out green and flat and perfect. Everything from the valley floor two hundred metres below had come out brown and brittle, and the papers were the same papers.
text_nonnarrative: Pressing and air drying are told apart by what constrains the specimen rather than by the agent that takes the water out: flat boards and pressure in the one, free circulation in the other. Colour retention belongs to the first class and shape retention to the second. Liquid preservation is a third class, apart from both in that the water is replaced and not withdrawn, and its products are not mountable on a sheet.

text_narrative: The first specimen goes into the relaxing jar on a Monday and comes out soft on the Thursday, which is ordinary. The second goes in the Monday following and comes out soft in an hour. The third comes out soft, and warm, and with its wings set at the very angle Teodoro was going to set them at, and the damp cloth in the jar is bone dry, and the jar has not been opened.
text_nonnarrative: Setting: the fixing of a dried specimen in a stated attitude with braces and card. Relaxing: the return of a dried specimen to a condition in which setting was possible, by exposure to saturated air in a closed vessel. Overrelaxed: the same specimen past the point at which the attitude held. Carded: set and mounted on card. Greasing: a separate defect, being the migration of fat to the surface, and no condition of the relaxing at all.

text_narrative: The skin on the workroom bench had been cased and turned by somebody who knew the work, and Halloran could not make it fit the label. The label gave a bird of the coast. The skin was thinned at the wing butts in the manner of the inland shops, salted rather than pickled, and sewn with a linen thread no coastal shop had bought in twenty years, and the tag was in the curator's own hand.
text_nonnarrative: Objections to dry preparation of skins mostly mistake a question of after-care for a question of method. A dry-prepared skin is stable in a dry room and unstable elsewhere, which is a claim about rooms. The habit of setting one method against another without stating the storage conditions is the real defect of the literature. None of that is an argument for the wet method. Its better contributions give the room first and the bench second.

text_narrative: A salvage party out of the northern shelters brings in forty hides off a store shut for a hundred and ten years. Thirty-nine are green-salted and hard as board. The fortieth is tanned through, supple, and stamped with a mark the shelters have no record of, and the salt on the other thirty-nine is dust dry, and the fortieth is the only hide in the lot with any water left in it.
text_nonnarrative: Reversibility was the mark that divided tanning from preserving, if the two were divided at all. Under salt the conditions for decay were absent and the substance was as it stood; under tan the substance itself was other than it had been, and the conditions were no part of the case. On that second account a tanned hide was not a preserved hide but a different material under one name.

text_narrative: When the long ships were first given leave to carry the dead of other worlds, a vault was cut into the keel of each and filled with spirit to the brim. The rule handed down was that nothing in a vault would change and nothing would be remembered. For eleven crossings this held. On the twelfth the jars in one keel stood clear and full and empty of all but spirit, and the vault was sealed.
text_nonnarrative: Spirit preservation was the maintenance of soft tissue in a bath of dilute alcohol, the bath being both the fixative and the medium of storage. Its stability depended on the concentration of the bath, which was subject to dilution by the water in the tissue itself. Colour was not within the scope of the method. Volume was. The ratio of bath to specimen was therefore the governing figure and was fixed by the water content of the class.

text_narrative: Two hundred years of drift and the wax in the vascular casts has not moved a micron, which is the point of wax, so there is nothing here for Ilinca to write up. Except that the casts are not the casts on the manifest. The manifest gives eleven arterial trees. There are twelve in the case, all injected in one hand, all from one donor code, and the twelfth is the finest work in the collection.
text_nonnarrative: Injection was an argument about what a preparation was for, and the argument was seldom made in the open. A cast was the geometry of a vessel and nothing of its wall, which was a real gain in one dimension and a real loss in another. Those who held for injection had the better of the demonstration and the worse of the record. That did not make the record the more important of the two.

text_narrative: There was a field on the wrong side of a hill where the clamps never froze, and the lord who held it clamped his roots there and nowhere else. His steward built a clamp in the good field one autumn to prove the story wrong. By the turn of the year the good clamp was ice to the heart and the wrong-side clamp was warm to the wrist, and the frost lay a foot deep on both.
text_nonnarrative: The field lay on a north slope at the foot of a long hill, with a spring line across its middle and rising ground on three sides. Clamps stood in two rows along the contour, the lower row on the wetter ground. Soil over the whole field was sand above clay, at a depth of some two feet. The hollow at the western corner was the last part of the field out of shadow.

text_narrative: In the fourteenth winter after the ash the deep store under the ridge was opened on the shortest day and the upper bins were found frosted to the third course. The store had held above freezing for thirteen winters on the heat of the ground alone. The council had the thermometers read hourly for a month, and every reading came back above freezing, and the frost went down a course a week throughout.
text_nonnarrative: Frosted produce means any root showing translucence or a watery separation of the flesh at any depth below the skin, whether or not the store is recorded as having held above freezing. Recorded temperature is evidence and not a definition. Translucence alone is sufficient. Where a bin contains frosted produce, the whole of the course in which that bin stands falls within the term. Nothing in this part affects roots damaged in the lifting.

text_narrative: The second pair are on the line and the ice under them is a hand thicker than the ice under the first pair, which the marker has measured and written down. Odile takes the first stroke. Her saw goes through eleven inches on the down stroke and comes up dry, and the kerf behind it closes white and holds, and the block will not float free although the cut is square all round.
text_nonnarrative: A cut counts only where the kerf is open along its whole length and the block stands free of the field. A block held by a closed kerf is no cut, and the pair holding it have no claim to a second line. Thickness of the field is a condition of the line and not of the cut, so a pair on thick ice are under the requirement of a pair on thin.

text_narrative: Nobody at the county show would enter against Wisniewski's peaches, and the year somebody did the whole class was struck off. She put up nine jars in wire-clip glass, which was not the glass in the schedule, and the steward let them stand. The challenger put up nine in ring glass and had the schedule and lost the table, and the class was gone from the list the following year.
text_nonnarrative: An entry is admissible in the sealed class only where the closure is of the ring pattern named in the schedule, and a wire clip places the jar in the open class whatever its contents. Nine jars are the unit of entry, and a short entry is admissible with the deficiency marked against it. A jar entered in the wrong class is not excluded; it stands in the class its closure gives it.

text_narrative: Halfway through the afternoon sweep the lower arm of the tower jams at forty-five and will not come down. Ilbert works the crank twice, feels the counterweight chain go loose in the housing, and leaves it. The arm above answers fine. He sends the whole word again with the upper arm alone, letter by letter, and the station down the ridge sends back the sign for a garble and nothing else.
text_nonnarrative: A jammed arm was a fault of the tower and never of the word it spelled. An arm held at forty-five counted as no letter at all, and the letter was read as absent rather than wrong. Slack in the counterweight chain bore on the cause and not on the class. Garble was the class where the upper arm alone sent a whole word, whatever the station on the ridge sent back.

text_narrative: For nine nights running that winter the middle hill of the chain went unwatched, and the keepers at either end of it never owned to knowing. The far end lit on the sixth night for a landing on the coast. The near end lit an hour later off its own reckoning of the smoke. Between them the middle hill stood dark, and the message crossed the county anyway, short by one fire.
text_nonnarrative: Six hills carry the chain along the ridge line, and the middle one is the lowest of them by a hundred feet. Its summit lies in the lee of the two on either side. Sightlines from the far end are clear to the coast and blocked inland. Ground on the near slope is boggy to the top, and the shelter for the watch sits below that, in a fold out of the wind.

text_narrative: There was a horn in the valley that would not sound a fifth, though it sounded every other interval a horn can. The smith who made it had been paid in salt and had counted the sacks twice. Three winters the calls went out short of one note, and the herds came in wrong to the wrong gates, and at the fourth winter a boy blew the fifth by accident and the hill answered it in a voice nobody owned.
text_nonnarrative: Gathering calls stand apart from warning calls in the interval they rest on rather than in their length. A warning rests on a fifth and holds it; a gathering rests on a third and holds no higher. Recall calls are a third kind, marked out from both by their want of any fixed interval at all. Pitch belongs to the horn and not to the class, so two horns a tone apart carry the same three calls.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the line the middle shutter of the sixth frame was found painted over on both faces. The station book for that quarter held no entry against it. Traffic that quarter ran at half the usual count and every word of it was clean. The overseer who came up in the autumn had the paint scraped off, and the count went back to its old figure with the old proportion of garbles in it.
text_nonnarrative: No frame was permitted more than six shutters, and the sixth was to be reserved for the numeral sign alone. Faces were required to be black on the near side and white on the far. Paint on a shutter was allowed only over rust and never over a working face. Where a frame stood within sight of two stations, its middle shutter was to be set for the nearer of them. Entries against a shutter out of use were required.

text_narrative: Nine of the eleven messages on the morning sheet come back repeated word for word, and Verrin cannot make that sit right. A clerk who repeats back perfectly nine times in a morning is a clerk who is copying from the sheet rather than from the wire. She marks the sheet with a cross in the margin and says nothing to the room. The tenth comes back with a fault in it, and she is almost glad.
text_nonnarrative: Repeat-back accuracy varies far more between clerks than between the hours of a shift. The median clerk returns about one message in seven with some fault in the repetition, and the middle half of the values lies between one in five and one in twelve. Clerks with the cleanest returns account for most of the spread rather than the worst, since perfect mornings are commoner in the sample than any run of ordinary ones.

text_narrative: A relay post on the third arm of the northern chain fell out of the circuit for six hours last quarter after its mast alignment slipped nineteen degrees. The two posts either side held the traffic between them at reduced rate. Crews from the coast reset the mast the same night. The interruption was logged as a single break and the messages held during it went out in their original order, none older than a day.
text_nonnarrative: Spacing between relay posts is a function of mast height and of the clarity of the air, and of nothing else in flat country. Where hills stand in the way, the governing quantity is the height of the obstruction rather than the distance. Each post holds a circuit with the two nearest to it and with no others. Without a working alignment at one post the two circuits either side of it are independent.

text_narrative: Before the hills had names the first watchers laid their fires nine leagues apart, and the smoke of them was the first speech the sky was made to carry. One column meant the sea was quiet. Two set a day's walk apart meant it was not. The wind, who had no part in the agreement, learned the spacing in a single season and began to lay false columns of its own along the eastern shore.
text_nonnarrative: Smoke signalling by column count is the coarsest of the visual codes, with a vocabulary fixed at four terms or fewer. Its unit is not the column but the gap between columns, measured in the spacing of the fires rather than in time. Legibility depends on a still air and on a sky pale enough to hold the outline. The code is therefore shallow, and its whole meaning is settled in advance.

text_narrative: Kesta learned the eastern frame in a fortnight and the southern in three days. The night the northern frame was rebuilt with two extra pigeonholes she threw eleven letters wrong in an hour. A month on she could work the new frame blind. The winter they turned the whole rack ninety degrees to the window she was slower than the boy who had started in October, and she stayed slower until spring.
text_nonnarrative: Throw: the placement of one letter into one pigeonhole, counted as a single act whatever its distance. Miss-throw: any throw into a hole adjacent to the right one. Foreign throw: the same fault at a distance of two holes or more, which is a separate class. Blind working: working a frame by the position of the hole alone. Rack turn: a change in the standing of a frame relative to the window.

text_narrative: The outer ring of the wheel turns without a sound, which is wrong, because the detents were cut by hand and every other wheel in the room clicks. Sabel holds it up to the lamp. Twenty-six letters on the inner disc, twenty-seven on the outer, and the twenty-seventh is a character she has never seen in any alphabet. She turns the ring one letter further. The extra character comes round again, in a different place.
text_nonnarrative: A pawl was absent from the smaller wheels, and on those the inner disc and the outer ring were free of each other at every setting. The larger pattern held three parts: a fixed plate, an inner disc lettered on its rim, and an outer ring seated over both. Detents lay under the ring at even spacing. The lettering on the two rims was of equal count on all but the courier pattern.

text_narrative: Nobody on the club's signal crew will hoist under Ferrow now, and it goes back to one race. He has a rule that the substitute flag stands for whatever the crew last sent, and he will not be argued out of it. The rule is right for two hoists in three. On the long numbers it puts a repeated digit one place out, and the whole board reads as a different boat, and that is what happens in the race.
text_nonnarrative: Substitute flags were always the shabbiest part of a hoist code, and the codes that leaned hardest on them were the ones that read worst at distance. What passed for economy in such a system was usually a refusal to buy a second set of numerals. The better codes were the ones that kept the substitute for a single position and never for a run, and even those were poor beside a plain second set of flags.

text_narrative: There was a house that kept its whole account in knotted cord, and a daughter of that house who could read a cord in the dark with one hand. When the cords were taken by a creditor she tied the same accounts again from memory in a single night. The knots came out identical but for one, and that one stood in the place where the creditor's own debt had been, and it counted for twice.
text_nonnarrative: The controversy whether a knotted cord was a record or a message turned on nothing in the cord itself. A record was held to be a thing that stood for a state; a message, a thing that stood for an act of sending. On that account one cord was both, and the two descriptions were not rivals but different ways of counting the same knots. The stronger view was that sending, and not the knot, made the difference.

text_narrative: In the sixth year after the market charter the holding shelf at the gate house was ordered emptied twice a year instead of once. Forty-one packets were burned at the first clearing and nine of them were claimed within the month. Two claimants brought their tallies and were told the tallies now stood for nothing. The clerk of the gate entered all of it under one line and gave the count wrong by three.
text_nonnarrative: A packet is held at the gate house only where no address within the town is given on it, and such a packet is said to lie at call. Where a claimant produces a tally answering to the packet, the holding ends and the packet is deliverable. Nothing in the clearing rule affects a packet under claim. A packet cleared from the shelf is not thereby undeliverable, but it is outside the holding.

text_narrative: Twenty flashes to the minute was the rate on the harbour lamp and Marnie had counted it since she was nine, lying at the top window with the sash up. Tonight it was nineteen. Nineteen was nothing, nineteen was a cold night and a stiff shutter, and she knew that, and she counted it again from the beginning and got nineteen, and lay there working out how long it would take anyone to notice.
text_nonnarrative: Beyond about thirty flashes to the minute a shutter lamp is unreadable at any distance, and below eight the rate is indistinguishable from an unsteady flame. Within those bounds the readable range varies as the inverse square root of the flash rate, and the constant of that relation is a property of the lens rather than of the shutter. The rate under cold is lower by roughly one flash in twenty for every ten degrees.

text_narrative: A station on the outer ring is answering to a call sign issued to a station decommissioned nine years ago, and traffic for both is arriving at the same receiver. The duplicate is not on any current list. Operators along the ring report clean signals in both directions and no loss of messages. The board has withdrawn the sign from service and assigned a third in its place, and the duplicate continues to answer.
text_nonnarrative: A call sign was valid only where it stood against a single station on the current list. Two stations answering to one sign made a position that was void, and neither answer counted. Silence was not an answer and could not be challenged. A sign withdrawn from service was unassignable for five years, and a station holding a withdrawn sign was out of the ring for every purpose but distress and the answering of it.

text_narrative: The three drums of the river people were cut from one tree in the age before the floods, and each was given a voice that reached a different distance. The smallest was heard to the first bend and no further. The middle one was heard to the falls. The great drum was heard by everyone the river had ever carried, living or otherwise, and for that reason it was struck once in a generation and never twice.
text_nonnarrative: Three sizes of river drum were in use, of which the middle was the commonest and the great drum the rarest by far. The small drum was a hand span across the head, hide on one face only, with the shell open below. The middle carried hide on both faces and a cord tension. The great drum stood waist high, was hooped in iron at the waist, and was mounted on a frame rather than carried.

text_narrative: Every capsule Ossian takes off a returning bird holds a message he has already had. The first time it is a note about a delayed cart, arriving four days after the cart. The second time it is the same note in the same hand. By the ninth bird he has stopped opening them and keeps the capsules in a jar, and the jar is heavier each week than the count of capsules in it will account for.
text_nonnarrative: Capsule weight was the wrong constraint to design a pigeon post around, and the codes built to respect it were poorer for the effort. The birds tolerated more than the designers allowed, and the saving in paper bought nothing but a denser hand and a higher garble rate. It was fair to grant that the lightest capsules did fly marginally better in wind. The gain sat well inside the loss in legibility, and the argument stood.

text_narrative: The far mirror answered before the near one had finished its word, which was not possible at that distance, and Peiro kept the sun on it anyway. Nine miles of dry air lay between the two stations. He tilted the mirror off the sighting rod and the answers went on coming, in the same hand, at the same rate. He put the cover over the glass. The last three letters arrived after the cover was down.
text_nonnarrative: Alignment is judged on the sighting rod and never on the answer received. A mirror off the rod is out of alignment whatever letters arrive, and a mirror true to it is in alignment though nothing arrives at all. Distance bears on the cause and not on the class: nine miles of dry air is within the ordinary reach. A cover over the glass puts the station outside the class entirely, since a covered mirror carries no sun.

text_narrative: Everyone on that street could read the chalk on the corner of the tannery wall, which was the trouble with it. A single upright meant a packet was lying under the third step. Two uprights meant the man who left it had been followed.
