For nine months the marks ran true, and then somebody who was not in the arrangement started chalking two uprights every night for the pleasure of watching the street empty.
text_nonnarrative: Upright: a single vertical stroke, the whole of the affirmative vocabulary. Crossed upright: the same stroke with a bar, meaning the affirmative was withdrawn. Blank wall: the state of a drop with no mark on it, which was distinct from a drop with a stroke rubbed out. Ghost: a mark whose maker was outside the arrangement. Wall hand: the manner of a maker, so far as it was legible in the stroke.

text_narrative: A heron of the marshes agreed to carry the line of a message kite from the low field to the headland, on condition that nothing be tied to it. The kite makers tied a slip of paper the width of a feather. The heron flew the line out to the headland as promised, and set it down, and never came back to the low field, and after that the kites were flown on the wind alone.
text_nonnarrative: Line for a message kite is required to be of hemp and of a single length, spliced nowhere along its run. A tail is permitted only on the smaller patterns. Signalling by line is to be read from the number of tugs and from their spacing, and no meaning is to attach to their strength. Where two kites are flown from one field, their lines are required to stand at least forty paces apart at the ground.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the siege the priority board at the north gate was reduced from five classes to two. Sixty-one messages sat in the middle class on the day of the change and every one of them was entered as ordinary. Four were for the water party. The runner who took them out went by the long lane, which was proper for ordinary traffic, and the water party had moved by the time he reached the ford.
text_nonnarrative: Priority was a property of the message and not of the runner who took it, and a message entered as ordinary was ordinary however it was carried. Classes were set at the board and nowhere else. The water party's traffic ranked by its content, so a class of two admitted no middle case and nothing was graded between them. The lane chosen out of the gate bore on the delay and never on the class of the message.

text_narrative: Two pads left in the tin and both of them numbered eleven, which means somebody at the other end has the same eleven, or nobody has. Sivrit turns them over. Same grain of paper, same ink, same worn corner. Either the printers duplicated a sheet forty years ago or the tin has been opened. He decides it was the printers, because the alternative asks who, and he has been careful not to ask that all winter.
text_nonnarrative: Security in a pad system rested on the pairing of sheets and on nothing in the characters themselves. Each sheet had exactly one counterpart, and the two were held at opposite ends of a single link. The numbering was an index to the pairing and carried no part of the key. Where a sheet existed in three copies rather than two, the pairing was undefined, and the system gave no account of which copy governed.

text_narrative: A listening watch kept at the northern depot last season recorded no traffic across eleven consecutive night shifts, the longest such run in the depot's record. The aerial and the receiver were found sound. The watch was kept by two members of the party in alternation, four hours each. Traffic resumed on the twelfth night at the usual volume, and the eleven blank sheets were entered in the log without comment.
text_nonnarrative: Inside the depot the listening room occupies the north corner, with the receiver bench against the outer wall and the log rack above it. The aerial mast stands forty paces upslope of the building, clear of the ridge to the east but not to the west. Ground between mast and door is gravel and holds no water. The bunk space lies through a single door, so the watch sits within call of the party.

text_narrative: In the years when the sky-writers still had their tower, every message was padded out to a thousand characters with nulls, so that no watcher below could count the length of a thing. The nulls were meaningless by decree. Then one of the sky-writers set the nulls of a whole season in a pattern, and the pattern was read from the ground, and the tower was pulled down by people who had learned to count.
text_nonnarrative: Nulls are called meaningless, and the word does more work than it can bear. A character carries no meaning under the code and yet carries information about the code, and these are two properties, not one. If the second counts as meaning, padding is a species of message and cannot be treated as absent. If it does not, the notion of meaning at work here is narrower than any ordinary use of the term.

text_narrative: Three times that year Delfa was handed a page reference with no book named, and three times she found the book by the shape of the numbers alone. The first was a psalter, from the low line counts. The second was an almanac, from the columns. The third had numbers that fitted nothing on any shelf in the house, and she carried it in her pocket for a month, and then she stopped carrying it.
text_nonnarrative: Running keys were not book codes at all, though the two were often lumped together: a running key drew its material in order, while a book code addressed it by position. Within book codes proper, the page-line-word form was distinguished from the word-count form by what the number indexed rather than by its size. A third form indexed the edition instead of the page, and was useless where two editions stood alike.

text_narrative: Fog on the channel and the whistle from the north bank gives four short and one long, which is not in the book. Aleth waits. The book has one short for a vessel under way, two for a vessel stopped, three for a vessel making sternway. Four is nothing. The whistle gives it again at the same interval, from a little nearer, and there is no vessel on the water between the two banks.
text_nonnarrative: An answering blast is legal only against a blast sounded from another vessel, and a vessel that answers nothing is in a position the code does not define. Four short blasts belong to no legal signal, so nothing answers them and the position stands unresolved. Silence from a vessel under way is a fault and not a signal. Two vessels sounding the same blast at once put both in the wrong, whatever their headings.

text_narrative: Nobody at the way station sets a clock by the down coach any more, and the reason is a driver called Herrick. He runs it early. Not late, early, which nobody expects and nobody can plan against, and the sacks go out before half the town has written. The company has spoken to him twice. He keeps the schedule to the minute on the up run, so there is nothing anyone can put in writing.
text_nonnarrative: A mail coach schedule was a table of latest permitted arrivals rather than of expected ones, which is why early running counted against it as heavily as late. Its intervals were fixed by the slowest stage on the route and not by the mean. Tolerance at each stage was narrow, of the order of a quarter hour, and the tolerance was one-sided. Punctuality was therefore a matter of the table and never of the road.

text_narrative: There was a scribe in the marsh country who could take down a speech faster than it was given, and the guild said it could not be done and sent for the outlines. The outlines were plain enough. Each stood for a word that had not been spoken yet. The guild burned the book and the scribe went on writing, and every speech in that country came out afterwards the way the outlines had it.
text_nonnarrative: Speed is the poorest ground on which to recommend a shorthand, and the systems that chase it are the least worth having. Economy in the tighter outlines amounts to a shifting of labour from the hand to the reader, who must supply half the vowels unaided. The systems worth defending are those legible to a second hand a year on, and these are without exception the slower ones to write and to learn.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the harbour works a lamp of the new pattern was set on the mole head, with four shutters instead of two. The keeper's return for the following winter showed the lower pair jammed on sixty nights and the upper pair on none. The founder was written to and did not reply. In the spring the lower pair was taken out altogether and the lamp worked as the old pattern had.
text_nonnarrative: Four parts make up a shutter lamp of the harbour pattern: the lantern proper, a pair of hinged leaves on either flank, a linkage behind them, and a hand lever at the base. The leaves are hung on pintles set into the frame and not into the glass. The linkage is single on the older lamps and doubled on the newer. A return spring is absent from every pattern with four leaves.

text_narrative: Sixty-two undelivered forms in the drawer and the disposal date is the end of the month, which Nerella has known for a fortnight and has done nothing about. Burning them is the rule. The rule assumes the addressees are gone, and eleven of these are for one house on the quay, and the house is not gone, it is only shut. She closes the drawer. There is a fortnight yet, she thinks, which is what she thought a fortnight ago.
text_nonnarrative: A message was undelivered where no addressee was found at the address borne on it, and undeliverable where no such address existed. The two were distinct and nothing in the disposal rule joined them. Where an address was found shut but standing, the message was undelivered and not undeliverable, whatever the length of the closure. Disposal applied to the undeliverable class alone, and nothing in it affected a message held against a shut house. Disposal date was no part of either class.

text_narrative: A correction sent from the eastern office this week reverses a figure that was never in error, and the original message is now on file in two forms. The office reports the correction as issued against the wrong serial. Both forms carry the same time of receipt. Clerks at the receiving end have entered the later form, as the standing arrangement provides, and the earlier one remains attached to the file unmarked.
text_nonnarrative: Corrections outnumber the garbles they answer to by about three to two across the offices sampled. Most of the excess falls to a small number of offices: five of the twenty-two account for over half of all corrections issued. Within an office the rate is steadier than between offices, and the spread over a year is narrow. Corrections against a wrong serial are rare, at under two percent, and they cluster in the same five.

text_narrative: When the first shaft was sunk the makers hung a bell at the head of it and gave the cage three strokes for down and two for up, and one stroke for a thing that had no name. In nine hundred years the one stroke was rung four times. Each time the cage came up empty and warm. The makers were long gone by the fourth, and the rope was rung by nobody anyone could find.
text_nonnarrative: Audibility of a shaft bell is proportional to the mass of the bell and inversely to the depth, though the second relation weakens below about forty fathoms. The number of distinguishable codes is bounded by the interval a listener can hold, which is of the order of four strokes. Beyond that the count is unreliable, and doubling the rope tension buys nothing, since the limit is in the listener and not in the bell.

text_narrative: Osher franked the first sack of the imperial mail with a die cut two days before the treaty and nobody questioned it. The second sack, in the spring, went out under the same die and came back from the border with every cover refused. He cut a new die in July with the old crown on it and that sack passed. In November the old crown was refused and the treaty die passed, and by then he kept both on the bench.
text_nonnarrative: A cover is refused on the die that struck it and never on the sack it travelled in. The crown borne by a die settles the class; the date the die was cut bears only on the cause of a refusal. A franking struck at the bench after a treaty is of the later class whatever crown it shows. Mail refused at the border is refused cover by cover, and a sack has no standing of its own under the rule.

text_narrative: The serial on the incoming slip read nine hundred and one, and the last one logged had been nine hundred and three. Teoline held the slip under the lamp with the log open beside it. Nothing was missing. Every number between was accounted for, signed, timed. She wrote nine hundred and one at the foot of the page, out of order, and drew a line under it, and the next slip came in reading nine hundred and one as well.
text_nonnarrative: Serial numbers were a poor guarantee of completeness, and the confidence placed in them was largely borrowed from the arithmetic rather than earned by the practice. A gapless run proved only that the numbers were gapless. Duplicates and reissues left no trace in the sequence at all. It was true that a gap was strong evidence of a loss, which was worth something. The converse did not follow, and most of the trust rested on the converse.

text_narrative: Everybody on the terrace knows what the green rocket means and nobody agrees about the red. Half the street holds it is a call for the boat crew. The other half holds it is the all-clear, which is the opposite thing, and both halves have been saying so since before Marda's mother was born. The chandler who sells the rockets will not be drawn. He sells more red than green, every year, and says nothing.
text_nonnarrative: Green, red, white and blue make up the whole of the chandler's stock, and green is the cheapest and the commonest by a wide margin. Green is a single star, burning about four seconds. Red is a single star of the same duration in a heavier case. White is a pair of stars with a half-second gap between them. Blue is the rarest and is sold only in boxes of six, with the case unmarked.

text_narrative: Seven posts stood on that road with a runner at each, and a tally stick split between every two of them so the halves had to meet. A runner at the fourth post lost her half in a river. She cut a new one and matched it to the third post's half, and it matched, and matched the fifth as well, and the road ran on for years on a stick that had never been split at all.
text_nonnarrative: A tally was in force between two posts only while both halves were in the hands of the runners of those posts, and not otherwise. Where a half was lost, the tally was void as between those two posts and unaffected as between any other pair. A half cut to replace a lost one was a new half and no part of the old tally. Nothing in the rule of replacement gave the new half the standing of the old.

text_narrative: In the third season of the packet run the speaking tubes were relabelled forward to aft instead of by deck, and the change was entered in the ship's book on a single line. For eleven days the calls went to the wrong stations. The mate who had ordered it kept a count and made the count seventy-four. On the twelfth day the old plates were screwed back over the new ones and the count stopped at seventy-four.
text_nonnarrative: Labelling a tube network by position rather than by function looks like the more durable scheme and is in fact the more fragile one. Positions hold only while the fittings do; functions survive a refit. The usual defence is that position needs no learning, and this is true of a newcomer on the first day. It is false of everyone else aboard, and the scheme is paid for daily by the many to spare the few.

text_narrative: Eleven strokes on the muster gong and the yard was full before the eleventh had finished, which was the part Ilva could not get past. Eleven meant assemble. Eleven had always meant assemble. But the yard had been empty at the first stroke and full at the tenth, and nobody had come through the gate, and she had been watching the gate the whole time because watching the gate was the whole of her work.
text_nonnarrative: A muster was counted from the gong and never from the yard. Eleven strokes stood for assemble whatever number of them was heard, so a count broken at the tenth was still eleven and still assemble. Presence in the yard bore on the return and not on the class of the call. The gate was no part of the criterion, and a watch kept at the gate the whole time settled nothing about who was mustered.

text_narrative: The counting office has ruled that a hyphenated compound stands as one word for charge, reversing a practice of nineteen years, and the ruling applies to traffic already lodged. Six hundred and forty messages lodged this week fall under it. The office states that no refund arises, since the earlier count was correct under the earlier rule. Clerks at four branches are entering both counts on the docket, which the ruling neither requires nor forbids.
text_nonnarrative: Every group of characters bounded by spaces was to be charged as one word, and a group of more than fifteen characters was to be charged as two. Figures were permitted in a group with letters only in an address. The signature was required to be charged and the address was not. Where a sender lodged a message with the count entered, the office was to accept that count unless it stood short by three or more.

text_narrative: In the age when the world was still plumbed with the old pipes, the makers left a tapping code in them so the deep places could answer the high ones. Three taps asked. Two answered. One was a refusal and could not be argued with. The pipes outlasted the makers by a great while, and the taps went on, and by the end nobody knew which end of the world was asking and which was refusing.
text_nonnarrative: Three taps constituted a question, and a question left standing for the space of a hundred beats lapsed and could not be revived. Two taps were an answer and were legal only where a question stood open. A single tap was a refusal, which was not an answer and could not itself be answered. A run of taps beyond three was no signal at all, and the line was held to be silent while it lasted.

text_narrative: The receipt book goes back to Tavi four times in one month with the same mark in it, a small circle. Nobody at that address will own to making it. The first time she takes it for a thumbprint. The second time she takes it for a coin rubbing. By the fourth she has stopped taking it for anything and just carries the book back and rules a line under the page.
text_nonnarrative: Hand receipt: a signature taken at the door from the addressee in person. Household receipt: the same, taken from anyone resident at the address, which was a lesser class. Mark: any sign other than a signature, valid where the maker was known to the carrier. Blind mark: a mark whose maker was unknown, which stood as no receipt. Refusal: the state of a delivery where no receipt of any class was obtainable.

text_narrative: The new chairs are wrong and Petra sees it as soon as she sets them by the fireplace wall. They are a twelfth of full size, and everything else in the room is a sixteenth, so the seats stand as high as the mantel shelf. She puts them in the box with the lid marked for the larger house. The room keeps its own furniture, four pieces, all cut from the same rule, and the gap by the hearth stays a gap.
text_nonnarrative: Scale error in a dolls house is graded on the room, not on the piece. A chair at a twelfth among furniture at a sixteenth is a fault of the room whatever the quality of the chair. Height against a fixed feature, the mantel shelf or a door head, is the mark that counts; the rule the maker cut to is a cause, not a class. Mixed size within one house is tolerated where the rooms are separate and the seats stand apart.

text_narrative: Nobody in the workshop would buy a miniature chest from Halloran, and it was not the finish. He cut his dovetails properly, at a twelfth of the size, and they held; what he would not do was cut them at all on the drawer backs, where nothing shows. Glued butt joints, every one, and half of them split inside a winter as the wood moved. The old hands said a joint that cannot be seen is the only one worth cutting.
text_nonnarrative: A miniature chest is graded on its hidden joints and not on its face. Dovetails at the drawer front count for nothing where the backs are butted and glued: the class of the piece is fixed by the weakest joint in it. Finish bears on the cause of a split and never on the grade. Wood movement across a twelfth-scale carcase is small, so a butt joint may hold for years, which is a matter of luck and not of class.

text_narrative: A model of a three-masted barque is entered at the harbour show with the standing rigging in one gauge throughout. The shrouds and the backstays are correct at the scale, but the ratlines are the same thread, which at a hundredth reads as heavy as the shrouds themselves. The maker states the hull took nine months. The model is placed second, behind a smaller ketch whose ratlines are drawn from a single strand of the same thread.
text_nonnarrative: Rigging was graded on the ratio between gauges and not on the absolute size of the thread. Shrouds heavier than ratlines was the required relation; equal gauge throughout was a fault whatever the accuracy of the hull. Hull work bore on the cause of a low grade and never on the class of one. A single strand drawn from a larger thread counted as a gauge in its own right, so a ketch and a barque were graded alike.

text_narrative: The masts in this bottle do not fold, and Corin cannot see how they went in. No hinge at the deck, no crease in the shroud lines, no thread through the neck and no wax where a thread would have been drawn out. The bottle is whole, the neck is a finger's width, and the hull is half again as wide. Somebody built it inside, over weeks, with tools he cannot picture, or else the glass was blown around it.
text_nonnarrative: A bottled ship was classed by the means of entry and not by the finish of the hull. A hinged mast, folded flat and raised by a thread through the neck, was the standard class. Wax at the neck bore on the cause of a stiff mast and never on the class. A hull wider than the neck with no hinge at the deck fell outside the classes, and glass blown around a model counted as a bottle only by courtesy.

text_narrative: Over four club nights Beatrix brought a different wagon to the same length of track. The first ran sweetly and was found to be a sixteen-millimetre body on a thirty-two millimetre chassis, which nobody minded. The second had wheels a shade too wide in the tread and picked every check rail on the curve. The third was correct in every dimension and derailed twice, on the same joint, for reasons the club never settled. The fourth she left at home.
text_nonnarrative: Gauge compliance is graded on the track and not on the body above it. A wagon whose wheel tread is wider than the standard is out of class whatever the accuracy of its body, since the check rail sets the limit. Body scale bears on appearance and never on the class: a sixteen-millimetre superstructure over a thirty-two millimetre chassis is admissible. Derailment at a single joint is a matter of the track and not of the wagon.

text_narrative: There was a maker of miniature railways who could not get a point to throw true, and a small man came to the door about it. He asked for the loan of the workshop for a night and for nothing else, and in the morning every blade on the layout sat tight against its stock rail. He had left a thread of hair under each tie bar, and the maker never dared lift one to look.
text_nonnarrative: Four throw distances are current in miniature pointwork, of which the middle two account for nearly all commercial track. The shortest is a sixteenth of an inch at the blade tip, found on tight radius units and prone to a loose fit against the stock rail. The longest, at three sixteenths, is proper to large scale garden work, where the tie bar is a visible member. Each is supplied with a spring or a solid bar.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the club layout the scenery committee changed from dyed sawdust to nylon fibre on the whole of the west end. The fibre was applied with a charged sieve and stood upright as promised, and the west end read as meadow for the first time. By the autumn the fibre had lain down flat wherever a sleeve had brushed it. The committee recorded the change as complete and ordered sawdust for the east.
text_nonnarrative: Three grades of ground covering are held in the club store, and the coarsest is the least used. Dyed sawdust is the oldest of them: flat in section, fast to apply, and indifferent to damp. Nylon fibre is supplied in two lengths, two and four millimetres, both charged before laying and both upright unless touched. Ground foam sits between the two, sold by the litre in four colours, of which the winter mix is the palest.

text_narrative: In the first making of small things, the shaper poured all his creatures on one tree of metal and left them joined at the ankle. Each had a seam down the length of it where the two halves of the mould had met, and the seam was the mark of the maker. The second shaper filed her seams away and cut her creatures free at the joint, and none of them could be told from the other.
text_nonnarrative: Sprue gates were made in three widths, and the narrowest was reserved for figures. The wide gate stood at the thickest part of a piece, was easy to cut and left a scar requiring filler. The narrow gate lay at an edge, took a blade cleanly and left a nick rather than a scar. Mould lines were a separate matter, present on every piece from a two-part tool and absent only from the slush cast forms.

text_narrative: The figure on the desk is a soft metal casting with the flash still on it, and Dolan turns it over twice under the lamp. Flash along the back seam, heavy, and a bright cut across the base where somebody has taken a blade to the mark. The mark is what he wants and the mark is gone. He sets it down beside the other four, all of them clean, all from a mould that nobody in this town owns.
text_nonnarrative: Collectors were too hard on flash and not hard enough on softness of detail. What was called a poor casting in the price lists was usually a well-cut one carrying flash that a minute with a blade would have removed, while a figure with rounded features, past saving, went unremarked. The best of the old writing on soft metal figures was the writing that held crispness and cleanliness apart. Base marks were a collector's concern and not a founder's.

text_narrative: Anybody who paints at the long table knows which figures are Ilse's, and nobody says so to her face. She lays four thin coats where the rest of the table lays one, and then floods the whole thing with a black wash that pulls it all back to grey. The work is beautiful in the hand and vanishes at arm's length. The old painter at the end of the table keeps one of hers on the shelf and does not explain why.
text_nonnarrative: Layering is overpraised in figure painting and washing is misunderstood. What is offered as depth in the club literature is usually a loss of contrast, since every added coat narrows the range between the highest light and the deepest shadow. A wash is the opposite instrument and is treated as though it were the same one: it darkens a recess without touching a raised edge. The strongest work in the form is meant to be seen at a distance, and it is thin.

text_narrative: A club tournament in the spring was decided on a hill built in four steps of card. The defending side held the top step and claimed cover from the step below it, and the attacking side claimed the same step as open ground. Neither reading was wrong under the printed rules, which spoke of slopes and not of steps. The organisers ruled for the defenders and rebuilt the hill in plaster before the summer meeting.
text_nonnarrative: Stepped terrain is defended for the wrong reason and attacked for the wrong one too. What is praised in it is legibility, which no rule set requires; what is held against it is unrealism, which is beside the point, since a step is a notation and not a hill. The better objection is that a step invites two readings of cover at once. Sculpted slopes are no answer, being harder to read and no less arguable.

text_narrative: The tower gives sixes and Tallin has stopped pretending otherwise. Three baffles, cut and glued by hand, nothing sprung, nothing weighted, and eleven sixes in fourteen throws with three different dice. A fault in the angles, then, or in the felt, or in the room. He turns the tower to face the window instead of the wall, throws again, and gets sixes, and sits with it in his lap for a while without throwing anything.
text_nonnarrative: No count of outcomes settled whether a dice tower randomised a throw or merely concealed it. If randomising was the claim, then a tower whose baffles returned one face more often than the rest was a bad tower, and the concept held. If concealment was the claim, the same tower was a good one and bias was no objection. The two claims answered to different demands, and neither was a degree of the other.

text_narrative: Every market day for a season the turner set out four tops on the same board. The first was true to the eye and fell inside a count of ten. The second was visibly lopsided and ran the longest of the four, which he could not explain to anyone who asked. The third he weighted with a lead pin at the tip and it walked off the board every time. The fourth he kept in his coat and never spun for anybody.
text_nonnarrative: Balance in a spinning top and symmetry in one are commonly treated as a single property, and they are not. Symmetry is a fact about the body at rest; balance is a fact about the axis under rotation, and a top can want the first and have the second. If the two were one property, a lopsided top would spin badly in every case, which is not what the word means. The confusion is old and survives in the trade term itself.

text_narrative: There was a magpie who stole a boy's yo-yo and could not make it come back up the string. She took it to the mole, who said the fault was in the axle, and to the hare, who said the fault was in the wrist. Both were right, and the magpie greased the axle with beeswax and never mastered the wrist, and so had a yo-yo that slept forever and rose never. She kept it anyway, in the nest, for the shine.
text_nonnarrative: Sleep in a yo-yo and return in one stood in tension rather than in sequence, and no single axle was right for both. If sleep was the end in view, then friction at the axle was a defect and a loose fit the ideal. If return was the end, friction was the whole mechanism, and a free axle a broken one. No account of the toy that took either end as the definition of the other could hold for long.

text_narrative: In the third year of the signal service the kite works bowed the cross spar of every standard kite to one part in twelve. The order came down after a season in which the flat-sparred kites had swung badly in gusts and the message flags with them. The bowed kites flew steadier and lifted less, and the service accepted the loss. A spar broken in bowing was recorded against the bender and not against the timber.
text_nonnarrative: Lateral stability varies roughly with the square of the bow depth, measured as the sag of the spar against its chord. The constant is a property of the covering rather than of the spar, so a paper kite and a silk one of the same frame do not compare. Lift is lower in the same proportion, though only as the first power of the depth. Past a bow of one part in eight the relation is lost.

text_narrative: The first kites of the cloud lords had no tails at all, and they went up like knives and came down like them. A servant of the least of those lords tied a rag of her own skirt to the foot of one. She added a second rag, and a third, and the kite hung steady over the tower for a day and a night. The lords took the craft from her and the rags with it.
text_nonnarrative: Drag on a kite tail is proportional to its length and to the square of the airspeed, and not to the weight of the cloth. The constant of proportion is a property of the material and of the width, so a narrow tail twice as long is not the equal of a broad one. Stability is greater with drag only up to the point at which the tail trails horizontally; beyond that, added length is dead weight.

text_narrative: In the long corridor of the orbital nursery the air is still and Pell throws the same folded glider eleven times. Flat wings, and it rolls out at the third window every throw. She creases both wings up by a thumb's width and it holds the centre line the whole length of the corridor and touches the far bulkhead. A minder tells her the corridor is not for throwing and she folds the wings flatter and throws again.
text_nonnarrative: Roll stiffness in a folded glider was proportional to the dihedral angle over the small range in which paper held a crease. The constant depended on the span and on the stiffness of the sheet, not on the weight at the nose. Above about ten degrees the relation reversed, since the outer panels shed more lift than they gained, and a glider folded to twenty degrees was less steady than a flat one. Wing loading bore on neither figure.

text_narrative: Everybody who worked in the bindery knew about the third plate of the garden book, and nobody would cut it. The pivot on that spread had been set a hair off centre in the first edition, and the arch it lifted always stood crooked, leaning to the gutter. Two binders straightened it and both found it crooked again the next morning with the glue dry. After that the plate was cut as drawn and the crookedness was called part of the design.
text_nonnarrative: A single-slit pop-up consists of a base sheet, a folded riser and two pivot tabs, one glued to each leaf. The riser is attached at the gutter fold and nowhere else, so its two arms stand as a pair of levers rather than as a hinge. Tabs are absent in the simplest cut-fold forms, where the riser is cut from the leaf itself. The slit lies across the gutter at right angles, and its length fixes the height of the arch.

text_narrative: A dealer's list for the spring sale describes a printed almanac with three volvelle discs, of which the middle one is missing. The remaining discs turn freely on a knotted thread through the centre and carry a full set of month names between them. The pointer, a separate strip of card, is present and loose in the gutter. The lot is withdrawn before the sale after a second reading of the collation, which calls for four discs and not three.
text_nonnarrative: A volvelle has four parts: a fixed ground printed on the leaf, one or more rotating discs, a pin through their common centre, and a pointer. The discs are stacked in order of size, the largest lowest, and each is attached only at the centre. In the simplest forms the edge of the upper disc serves as pointer and none is fitted. Tabs at the rim are proper to the larger discs alone and stand clear of the printed scale.

text_narrative: The cut is not a cut Wren has seen before and the box has no maker's name on it. Every knob on every piece is the same knob, to the thousandth, which no steel rule die will do after the first few hundred impressions. Unless the die is not steel. She fits four pieces together and they hold without pressure, as though the board had been grown in one and parted afterwards along lines it already had.
text_nonnarrative: A cutting die for jigsaws had three members: a plywood base board, the steel rule set into it on edge, and rubber ejection strip between the rules. The rules stood proud of the base by the thickness of the puzzle board and no more. Each interlocking knob was a single bend in one rule, so the knob of one piece and the socket of its neighbour were one member. Ejection rubber was absent in the earliest dies.

text_narrative: Three sets came through the house that winter and none of them squared up. The first was cut from a board that had shrunk across the grain, so the large triangles met at the hypotenuse. The second was true but the small square was thicker than the rest and sat proud of the tray. The third was bone, cool to the hand, and made the square, the rectangle and the parallelogram without argument, and it was the one that went missing.
text_nonnarrative: The seven pieces of a tangram set were carried on a single square, and every dimension in the set was a function of that square's side. The two large triangles were each a quarter of it; the parallelogram, the small square and the medium triangle each an eighth. Thickness was independent of the plan, so a set true in outline could nonetheless be uneven in the tray. Without a tray the pieces stood in no fixed relation at all.

text_narrative: There was a joiner who built a marble run down the whole stairwell of a tall house, and it ran for as long as anyone cared to watch. He had set every chute at the same shallow fall, one in forty, and the marbles kept their speed from the top landing to the hall. The house was sold twice and the run was never taken out, and the children of the second buyers said the marbles came back up at night.
text_nonnarrative: A marble run is carried on a series of chutes, each hung at its head and resting on the next at its foot. Terminal speed on a chute is a function of the gradient and of the rolling resistance of the surface, and not of the length. At one in forty on planed wood the two are in balance and the speed is steady. Without a lip at the outer edge the chute holds the marble only below a certain speed.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the tin works the barrel of the standard motor was changed from an open form to a closed one. The open barrels had been cheap and had thrown their springs whenever a child overwound them, and the works had replaced eleven hundred in a single quarter. The closed barrels held, and the same child broke the key instead. The works recorded the change as a saving and the key as a consumable part.
text_nonnarrative: Three barrel classes are recognised in tin clockwork, and the third is a hybrid. The open barrel is distinguished by what it lacks rather than by what it holds: no cap, no arbor collar, and the spring visible along its whole length. The closed barrel is marked by the cap alone; wall thickness and spring gauge bear on neither class. The half-closed form belongs to both and to neither, since its cap is pierced and the spring shows through it.

text_narrative: In the age when the makers gave motion away, three gifts were made to the children of the plain. The first was a wheel that turned while a hand turned it, and it was honest and dull. The second was a wheel weighted at the rim that ran on after the hand was lifted, and it was the one the children kept. The third turned forever and was taken back, and the makers left no account of where it went.
text_nonnarrative: Two drive classes were held apart in tin toys, and a third stood between them. The friction drive was distinguished by the absence of any store of motion: gearing to the road wheels and nothing else. The flywheel drive was marked by mass at the rim, which was a store, and so ran on unaided. Spring drive belonged to neither, its store being in strain rather than in motion, and it was graded by winding rather than by weight.

text_narrative: The lid is shut and the catch is home and Adalin can hear the spring shift inside anyway. She holds the box on her knees in the attic light and counts to sixty, and at fifty-one the lid lifts a quarter inch and settles back. The catch has not moved. She carries the box down to the yard and leaves it on the wall, shut, and it is still shut in the morning and the spring is quiet.
text_nonnarrative: Inside the box the spring lay coiled against the floor, filling the lower two thirds of the cavity. The figure sat on top of it, head under the lid and knees to the front wall. The catch was on the right, a bent wire through the wall an inch below the rim, with its hook to the inside. The crank hole was in the left wall, low, and nothing stood between it and the spring.

text_narrative: The horse in the front room had been in the house longer than anyone in it, and it did not rock evenly. Everybody who grew up there learned to sit forward of the girth, because the bow was heavier at the tail end and would tip a rider back into the window ledge otherwise. Two generations sat forward without being told why. When it went for repair the bow came back matched and nobody liked it as much.
text_nonnarrative: On the bow the horse stands well forward of centre, the girth over the front third of the span. The two rockers lie parallel, four inches apart at the head and the same at the tail, with a stretcher under the belly. The deeper part of each curve is aft, so the low point of the arc sits behind the rider. A footboard is at the front only, and the floor under the tail end is the more worn.

text_narrative: A cottage workshop in the northern valleys was recorded in the spring as turning four thousand peg dolls in a season. Of these, the smallest were turned by the youngest hand at the lathe and were shorter by a quarter inch than the pattern. The buyer took the whole season's work at the agreed rate and sorted it afterwards by height in the warehouse. The short dolls were sold in the same boxes at the same price and no note was made of them.
text_nonnarrative: Height in turned peg dolls varied more within a single workshop than between workshops. In the sample taken across the valleys, the median was three and a quarter inches, with a spread of half an inch either way. The hand at the lathe accounted for most of that spread; the timber and the season for very little of it. Some twelve percent fell short of the trade pattern, and shortfall was commoner in the smaller shops, where one turner did all the work.

text_narrative: The arms are strung too tight and Marta knows whose work that is without looking at the mark on the neck. Elastic at that tension holds a pose for a year and then goes brittle, and the doll comes apart at the shoulder in a drawer somewhere with nobody touching it. Which is exactly what happened to the last one. She slackens the cord half a turn and hangs the doll on the rail with the others.
text_nonnarrative: Cord tension at stringing varied more between makers than between the sizes a single maker produced. Across the recorded workshops the median tension was enough to hold a raised arm for some two years, and a quarter of the sample held for less than one. Maker accounted for most of the spread; cord material for a little and doll size for almost none. Failure at the shoulder was reported four times as often as failure at the hip.

text_narrative: Over the winter in the tower the boy made four drums for the same strip of pictures. The first had slits a finger wide and the figures smeared into one another at speed. The second had slits cut with a razor and the picture was sharp and so dark that only the lamp behind it made it out. The third he cut between the two and it worked, and the fourth he never finished because the strip wore through at the join.
text_nonnarrative: A zoetrope was a slotted drum characterised by the ratio of slit width to picture width rather than by its diameter. Its resolution depended on that ratio and on nothing else in the design: a narrow slit gave a sharp image and a dim one, a wide slit the reverse. The usual proportion was a fortieth of the circumference, which was a compromise and was known to be one. Illumination was therefore external and strong, and the drum interior was pale.

text_narrative: There was a card painter who put a bird on one side of a disc and an empty cage on the other, and sold it at fairs. A woman bought it for her daughter and the child spun it and the bird was in the cage, and would not come out again however slowly the disc was turned. The painter would not take it back and painted no more cages after that season.
text_nonnarrative: A thaumatrope is a two-sided disc characterised by images that are complementary rather than sequential, which distinguishes it from every other spun toy. Its effect depends on the persistence of the eye and on the axis of spin, since the two faces must present the same way up. One image is therefore inverted in the painting, and the pair is fixed for a single direction of rotation. Threads at either edge are the usual drive.

text_narrative: In the year the guild admitted small work, the warden set the limit for a bound miniature at one inch across the board. Three of the four books entered that autumn were over it by a sixteenth and were shown outside the case. The fourth, at seven eighths, had a sewn headband no thicker than a hair and took the guild's ribbon. The limit was written into the book of the guild the following spring and never altered.
text_nonnarrative: A bound miniature is required to measure not more than one inch on the greater dimension of the board. Sewn structures are permitted at any size; adhesive spines only below three quarters of an inch. The headband, where present, is to be worked in silk and is not to stand above the head of the board. Boards are to be of paper or of thin wood, and leather over board is required in the closed class.

text_narrative: When the first station was hung above the world, its builders made a window that looked on a garden. The garden was three feet deep and read as a mile, because the trees at the back were a fortieth of the trees at the front and the path narrowed all the way to a painted hill. Every child born there believed in the hill, and none of them could say afterwards when they had stopped.
text_nonnarrative: Depth in a forced diorama was required to be graded in not fewer than four planes. A scale ratio of more than one to three between adjacent planes was not permitted, since the step read as a step. The rear plane was to be painted and was not to carry a modelled figure of any size. Viewing was permitted from one aperture only, and the aperture was to be fixed in height and not adjustable.

text_narrative: At the kitchen table Rosalind twists sixty strands of florist wire into a trunk and splits them off in threes. The lower branches come out fine and the crown runs out of wire, so the top of the tree is four bare stems where there should be forty. She adds a second bundle at the fork and binds the join with thread. The tree stands in the vice overnight with the join at eye level, plain as a splice on a rope.
text_nonnarrative: Wire armatures were the wrong method for model trees and the only practical one. The objection to them was structural: the number of strands had to be settled before the first twist, and no number settled that early could match the branching of a crown. Against this it was often said that a modeller could add a second bundle of wire at any fork. So a modeller could, and the join showed at every attempt, and the objection stood unanswered.

text_narrative: The duck on wheels that went round the estate for thirty years was never quiet and never the same twice. Whoever had it would swear the clack changed with the weather, faster in the dry, slower and heavier when the rain came, and nobody ever oiled it. It went through nine families and came back to the first one with the cam worn to a smooth oval that should not have clacked at all. It clacked.
text_nonnarrative: The clacking pull-along is dismissed as a noise toy, and the dismissal misses the mechanism. Noise is the effect but not the function: the cam under the axle converts steady rolling into an irregular beat, and the irregularity holds attention where a bell would not. It may be objected that the beat is regular after all, being fixed by the cam. Fixed it is, and irregular against the walking of the child, which is the frame that matters.

text_narrative: A parlour skittles set entered for the county fair was measured on the morning of the second day. Eight of the nine pins stood to the pattern; the ninth was heavier at the base by two ounces of sand under a plugged foot. The owner said the pin had been rebuilt after a split and the sand was there for weight and not for advantage. The set was shown as a working set and not as a matched set.
text_nonnarrative: Ballast: any weight added inside the foot of a pin after turning, whether of sand, shot or plaster. Plug: the disc closing the cavity, flush with the foot and of the same timber as the pin. Matched set: nine pins of which no two differed in weight by more than half an ounce. Working set: any set outside that tolerance but sound in foot and head. Dead pin: one whose ballast had shifted and lay loose in the cavity.

text_narrative: Three rods for two arms, and Enid has counted them twice against the screen. The elbow rod is the one that should not be there, because this figure was cut with the elbow fixed and she cut it herself in the spring. Somebody has pierced the joint and set a rod in it, and the pierce is clean and old. She works the new rod once and the shadow arm bends the wrong way at the elbow, backwards, like nothing that walks.
text_nonnarrative: Control rod: the fixed stave at the trunk, carrying the whole weight of a figure. Action rod: any rod at a limb, jointed to it at one end and free at the other. Live joint: a pierced joint with an action rod fitted, the limb turning about the pierce. Dead joint: the same pierce with no rod, or a joint cut solid in the hide. Reverse: any live joint whose travel lay outside the range of the joint it stood for.

text_narrative: Across three exhibitions Nell shows the same window at a twentieth scale and is asked the same question at each. At the first the panel is leaded in drawn wire and the steward enters it under glass. At the second the wire is flat-rolled and the steward enters it under metalwork. At the third the panel is unchanged and the steward asks her which she would prefer, and she says glass, and it goes under glass and takes nothing.
text_nonnarrative: A leaded miniature means, in this schedule, a glazed panel under nine inches in either dimension in which the calmes are of lead or of lead alloy. Drawn wire of round section does not fall within the definition, and a panel so made is entered as metalwork. Where a panel carries both round wire and flat calme, the greater length by measure governs. Nothing in this schedule affects the classification of painted glass carrying no calmes at all.

text_narrative: There was a saddler's widow who stuffed hobby horse heads with horsehair and would use nothing else. A fox came to the door in a coat and offered her a sack of wool at half the price, and she took it, and the heads went soft inside a month and hung on their sticks like sacks. She bought no more wool, and the fox was seen at the next village with a sack of horsehair.
text_nonnarrative: A stuffed head means a hobby horse head filled with a resilient material, resilience being recovery after compression and not density. Horsehair, tow and curled paper are within the definition; wool and rag are not, being non-resilient however tightly packed. Where a head is filled with two materials, the material at the muzzle governs. Nothing in this part applies to a head of carved wood, which is not a filled head at all.

text_narrative: In the third year of the camp the model club fixed the rib spacing for hull work at four matchsticks to the inch. Two entries that season were built at three and were shown but not entered, and one at six collapsed under its own deck before the show. The four-stick rule held for the rest of the war and was written on the workshop wall in pencil. Nobody recorded who set it.
text_nonnarrative: A hull was admissible only where the rib spacing lay between three and five sticks to the inch. A hull outside that band stood outside the class and could not be answered by a hull inside it. Spacing was counted at the widest frame and nowhere else, so a tapered hull was legal on one count and not on another. Collapse under deck weight was a defect of the joint and bore on no rule.

text_narrative: In the time before hair was given to the made people, their heads were painted and their makers were content. One maker, the least of them, knotted a single strand through a pierced scalp and drew it tight, and then another, and did not stop for nine days. The made thing she finished was the first to be wept over, and the others were put away unfinished. After that no head was painted again.
text_nonnarrative: A knot counted as set only where it lay flat against the scalp and held against a pull of one ounce. Two strands through a single pierce were not two knots and could not be counted as such. A scalp in which the pierces stood closer than a sixteenth of an inch was void, whatever the number of knots in it. Painted hair was not hair and was answerable to no rule of knotting at all.

text_narrative: Halfway along the third length of channel Merin set the boning rods down and squinted at the sight line. The gradient wanted one in four hundred and the masons had given him one in six hundred over two bays, so the water would stand instead of run. He chalked the offending stones, lifted the level again, and marked the bed for lowering before the mortar took. Two courses would come up again before the week was out.
text_nonnarrative: Slack gradient, not rough stone, is what disqualifies a length of aqueduct channel. A bed laid at one in six hundred falls into the standing class whatever the finish of its stones; a bay steeper than one in two hundred falls into a second class, scouring rather than standing. The sight line and the boning rods bear on the cause of either fault and never on the grade class itself. Mortar is immaterial. Water depth is not a criterion.

text_narrative: Nobody in the low parish trusts the belly of the old siphon, and there is a reason. Every thaw it clogs, and every thaw the ganger Perrit walks the invert with a lantern and comes up grey to the elbow. This spring he finds a hoop of river weed packed round something that hums. He leaves it there, blocks the chamber, and tells the wardens the pipe is minded now and wants no cleaning.
text_nonnarrative: Silt deposits in a siphon belly were sorted into two kinds, and the sorting was by grain rather than by bulk. Coarse charge, meaning sand and grit heavy enough to lie where it settled, was one kind; the fine charge, held in suspension and let down only in slack water, was the other. Weed counted as a third class, distinguished from both by being organic and by lodging at the bends, not the low point.

text_narrative: The works committee of an inland borough recorded a short stoppage at its settling tank last April. A timber baffle in the second compartment tore loose from its brackets during a heavy inflow and lay across the outlet channel for eleven hours. Turbid water passed to the filters in that time and two beds were taken off. A carpenter refitted the baffle in oak the following week and the brackets were doubled.
text_nonnarrative: Baffles in a settling tank are carried on brackets set into the side walls, one course above the sludge line. Their spacing is a function of tank length and of the intended fall in velocity, not of depth. Where the inlet is central, the first baffle stands nearer the head wall than the rest. Without a baffle the inflow and the outlet channel are hydraulically continuous and the compartments are nominal.

text_narrative: There was once a city that kept its water clean by a grey skin on the sand, and a filterman named Odarr who was paid to leave it alone. Twice a year he scraped it off and buried it under the willows, and twice a year it came back thicker. In the dry year it did not come back, so he carried a pail of pond scum up the embankment and sowed it like barley.
text_nonnarrative: A slow sand filter was a bed of graded sand, two or three feet deep, characterised less by the sand than by the biological skin at its surface. Its clarifying power was held to depend on that skin and on a low rate of passage, of the order of a few inches an hour. Working depth was therefore shallow and fixed by the head available above the sand. Coarse beds of the same depth were a different class.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the new works the gravel came from a pit two valleys off, and the entry for that autumn was brief. Three barge loads were rejected at the wharf for want of screening, the smallest stones being mixed through the largest. The engineer to the works ordered the whole delivery washed and sized again on the bank. Laying of the under-drains was held over until the frosts.
text_nonnarrative: Gravel under a filter bed was to be laid in four sizes, coarsest at the bottom and each layer twice the grain of the one above it. Screening at the pit was required, and unscreened stone was permitted only in the lowest layer, where the under-drains were bedded. No layer was to be thinner than three inches. Sizing on the bank counted as compliance where a pit had no screens.

text_narrative: Quarter to six, and the standpipe at the court end will run for forty minutes if the pressure holds. Bettris counts the pails in the passage and thinks the tally wrong again. Four households, eleven pails, and the woman from the top floor never comes down before the tap is off. There is no sense arguing it at the pump; the hours are chalked on the wall and the chalk is not hers to change.
text_nonnarrative: Chalked hours: the intervals during which a standpipe was under pressure, as posted at the head of a court. Dry interval: any period outside those hours, whether or not the main was charged. Pail right: the number of vessels allotted to a household within one interval. Short hour: a chalked interval curtailed by low pressure, and counted at its posted length rather than its actual one. Standing pail: a vessel left at the tap between intervals.

text_narrative: Three summers the carter Ilsom worked the dry side of the county. The first year he made two rounds a day to the ranch tanks. The second the creek held longer and he added a third round, selling by the barrel at the crossing. The third the wells at the crossing failed and he hauled from the spring nine miles out, once a day, and raised the price twice.
text_nonnarrative: Carted water accounts for a small share of rural supply, but the share varies more between dry districts than between wet ones. The median haul in the sample is about six miles and the spread is wide at the upper end. Distance, not cart size, accounts for most of the variation in the price charged by the barrel. Households on shared tanks report fewer rounds a week than those without.

text_narrative: When the first cisterns were set on the roofs of the high city, the makers left in each a pipe that spoke. It stood a hand below the rim and ran out through the wall, so that any cistern filled past its measure wept into the street below. The eldest of the makers, Havel of the leaden trade, set his own pipe an inch lower than the rest and was mocked for it a hundred years.
text_nonnarrative: Above the working level of a domestic cistern there are two openings, and they are not alike. The lower is the warning pipe, of small bore, carried through the wall to a visible point outside. The upper, where present, is a vent, open to air and not to fall. In the smallest cisterns the vent is absent and the warning pipe doubles as one. Both are independent of the inlet and its valve.

text_narrative: The tank room over the empty ward is cold, and the ball valve is hissing again. Sennick lifts the lid and finds the float arm cocked upward, held as if a hand were under the copper ball, though the water stands four inches short. He bends the arm down. It rises again while the lid is still in his hand, and the hissing stops, and the level in the tank does not change.
text_nonnarrative: A defective ball valve was classed by where it stood open, not by the noise it made. Closure short of the working level, with the float arm high and the copper ball dry, was one class; closure only at the arm's limit, the water standing over the rim, was another. Hissing bore on neither class, being common to both. The lid and the tank itself were outside the classification altogether.

text_narrative: Old plumbers in the quarter would not let a lad wipe a joint until his third winter, and the reason went back to Corriel the elder. He wiped the main run under the abbey kitchen in a single afternoon, showing off, and every joint of the nine held for forty years but the last. That one wept a spoonful a day into the cellar sand, and nobody ever found it, and it was left weeping.
text_nonnarrative: Under the older ordinances a wiped joint meant a union in lead made solid with solder worked by cloth, and no other union in lead qualified. Where a joint lay in a covered run, the standing of the workman was material to its acceptance and the number of joints was not. Nothing in that provision affected joints in other metals, which were governed under a separate head and to a different standard.

text_narrative: A night inspector for the water board reports finding nine stopcock boxes open on one street of the harbour quarter. The covers are gone, the spindles are turned off at seven of the nine, and a strip of felt is packed into each box to keep the key from ringing. Two chandlers on the same street lose their supply before dawn. The board offers a reward and the inspector is moved to another district.
text_nonnarrative: Only a sworn officer of the board was competent to turn a stopcock at the pavement, and competence was in the office rather than in the key. A box left uncovered was a breach whoever had opened it. Turning off a supply for arrears was lawful; turning it off for a complaint was not, and no complaint made the first lawful. The felt packing was neither an offence nor a defence to one.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the district's mains the flushing book showed a gap of nine weeks in the eastern round, the ganger for that quarter being short of two men. Discoloured water was drawn at four houses and the committee ordered the round doubled until the year's end. The book for the following spring showed the eastern hydrants opened every fortnight, and the western ones left on the old interval.
text_nonnarrative: Scour velocity at a hydrant is proportional to the square of the outlet diameter for a given head, so a small increase in bore is worth more than a long opening. The constant of proportion is a property of the main's roughness and not of the hydrant. Below a velocity of about two feet a second the relation is of no practical interest, since deposit is not lifted at all.

text_narrative: Forty feet of head, and the upper tiers of the habitat still draw nothing. Ivrin stands at the tower gauge and thinks the arithmetic of it, which has not changed since the tower was cast. Nobody built the third tier expecting the same tank to serve it. The gauge is honest, the pumps are honest; it is the tier that is a lie, and the council will want the gauge blamed.
text_nonnarrative: Pressure at a draw-off point is a function of the vertical distance to the water surface in the tower and of nothing else at rest. Friction in the mains subtracts from it only while water is drawn. A tower serving tiers of different height gives unequal pressure at each, and the highest tier is the worst served. Boosting sets are independent of the tower and are rated separately.

text_narrative: Each dry month the keeper Marsal goes down to a lower valve. In the first month she draws from the top gate and the water is warm and green. In the second the top gate stands clear of the surface and she takes the middle. By the fourth she is on the bottom draw-off, tasting silt, and she chalks the date on the gatehouse wall beside three older dates in another hand.
text_nonnarrative: Three draw-off gates lay in the face of the gatehouse tower, one above another, the topmost eight feet under the spill level. The valley floor behind was silted to within a yard of the lowest gate. Water at the tower was deepest along the old stream line and was shallowest towards the northern arm, which was reed to the bank. The gatehouse itself stood on the dam and not on the shore.

text_narrative: The river had a right before the city had a wall, and the founders knew it. When they closed the gorge with earth they left a notch in the sill, a hand deep and four paces wide, through which the river drank its own portion for ever. In the third generation a governor filled the notch to gain a summer's water, and the river was said to have taken the same measure back out of the earth.
text_nonnarrative: Whether a compensation flow was a debt owed to the river or a mere reservation from the city's own store was disputed in the older writing. On the first view the water was never the city's to hold, and a dry channel below a dam was a wrong independent of any loss to mills. On the second the flow was a charge on property, and its measure was a matter of arrangement rather than of right.

text_narrative: A carpenter of the upper glen was paid in fish for keeping the leat sound, and he kept it with larch. There was one launder over the ravine that no timber would hold, and each spring he set a new trough there and each autumn found it split end to end. In the ninth spring he set an old one that had been in his father's shed, and it neither split nor leaked.
text_nonnarrative: Three timbers are in common use for launders, of which larch is the commonest and oak the dearest. Larch troughs are sawn in lengths of twelve feet, half-lapped at the joint, with a fillet along each upper edge. Oak is used only at the crossings, in shorter lengths and thicker stuff. Elm is the third, cheap and short-lived, and is found on temporary leats and on the tail lengths below a sluice.

text_narrative: Down in the shaft the youngest of the steiners works by candle, laying the brick without mortar, ring by ring, and the ring above him is out of true by half an inch. Water comes in at the third course from the bottom, cold enough to numb a wrist. He wedges an oak slip behind the leaning brick and sets the next ring hard against it, and the shaft closes true above his head.
text_nonnarrative: Dry steining is admired for the wrong reason. What passes for craft in the accounts of it is usually mere patience, the laying of ring upon ring in a wet shaft; the real difficulty is the setting-out at the bottom, where half an inch of lean is carried up the whole depth. Descriptions that dwell on the candle and the cold are the least useful. The best of them treat the first three courses and stop.

text_narrative: Everybody on the common knows which wellhead slab is the wrong one, and nobody lifts it. It sits a finger higher than the other four, and the grass round it grows in a ring. Old Pethick tells it that the slab was cut from a lintel and remembers being a lintel, and that a stone which remembers a door will act like one. The parish keeps a second bucket for that well and uses the first.
text_nonnarrative: Covering a well was always more a matter of custom than of engineering, and the customs were better than the engineering deserved. A jointed cover of four or five slabs was harder to seal than a single stone, yet it was commoner, because a single stone of that span was beyond the lifting tackle of most parishes. Against that it may be said that jointed covers were the ones most often left ajar, which was the graver fault.

text_narrative: A county surveyor's return for one upland parish described the failure of a windlass over a public well in the market square. The barrel split along an old shake under a full bucket and the crank ran back, throwing the rope clear of the drum. No injury was reported. The well was ordered closed with planks for a fortnight, and a wheel and chain were fitted in place of the barrel.
text_nonnarrative: Hand-drawn wells fell into three classes by their lifting gear rather than by their depth. The plain rope well, with neither drum nor wheel, was the shallowest class and the commonest. A windlass well was distinguished from it by the barrel and crank, which gave purchase but held the rope in one plane. The wheel-and-chain well made a third class, marked off from both by carrying the load on a chain.

text_narrative: A jackdaw kept house in the frame of a chain pump for four seasons and made something of each. In spring she took the wool caught on the rising discs and lined the crossbeam with it. In summer she rode the slack chain down and back for want of anything better. In autumn she hid barley in a slot in the trunk. In winter the pump was worked daily and the barley came up wet.
text_nonnarrative: A chain pump is a lifting device in which discs on an endless chain are drawn up a close-fitting trunk, each disc carrying the column of water above it. Its delivery depends on the fit of disc to trunk and on the speed of the chain, and hardly at all on the depth. Leakage past a worn disc is therefore the governing defect, and the useful lift is short and fixed by that fit.

text_narrative: In the second year after the treaty the downland villages were required to hold their own water, and the entry for the ninth pond was the fullest. The clay was puddled by six oxen driven in circles for two days, and a layer of straw was laid under it against the frost. Rain filled the pond by the feast of the harvest. By the next summer it held two feet and the straw had not rotted.
text_nonnarrative: A sound dew pond was judged on the clay and on the straw layer under it, and not on the water it held in a wet summer. Clay puddled thin, meaning under nine inches, was disqualifying whatever the depth standing in the pond. Straw omitted was a separate fault, bearing on the frost and never on leakage. Rain in the year of making was material to the cause of failure only, not to the class of it.

text_narrative: The first minute of rain was the minute that mattered, and Aunt Corrance had never once let it into the butt. She stood at the downpipe with the swing spout turned to the garden and counted, roughly, by the sound on the slates. Soot, moss, whatever the sparrows left. Then the spout across, and the good water in, and the lid down before the leaves could follow it. Her tea was famous in that street.
text_nonnarrative: Foul flush: the first water off a roof after a dry spell, carrying the soot and dust lodged on the slates. Swing spout: a downpipe fitting with two positions, one to waste and one to the butt. Clean run: any water after the foul flush, and by convention only after the first minute. Butt charge: the quantity standing in a butt, exclusive of the sediment below the tap. Waste position: the spout setting that discards the flush.

text_narrative: The grid over the gutter mouth was clear when Halven went up the ladder, and by the time he reached the second bracket it was packed solid with beech leaves, wet and set in a spiral. He cleared it with a gloved hand. Below him the downpipe swallowed once and went quiet. On the way down he passed the grid again and it was packed, in the same spiral, and there was no beech tree near.
text_nonnarrative: A leaf grid has three parts: a rim that beds in the gutter mouth, a cage of wire or cast bars, and in the larger patterns a hinged flap at the crown. The rim is the only part fixed to the gutter; the cage stands proud of it by two or three inches. In domestic sizes the flap is absent and the crown is closed. The downpipe carries no part of the grid.

text_narrative: Before the makers learned the egg, the drains of the old capital were round, and the round drains kept nothing moving in the dry months. It was said that a mason dreamed of a bird standing on its narrow end and woke knowing the shape of a sewer. He cut the first egg section in the year of the low river, narrow below and wide above, and the city walked over it without knowing.
text_nonnarrative: Two claims are run together in the usual defence of the egg-shaped sewer. One is geometric: a narrow invert gives greater depth for a small flow, and depth is what carries solids. The other is structural: the section is stronger against ground pressure than a circle of equal area. If the first holds, the shape is a hydraulic argument and the strength is incidental. If only the second holds, the reasoning is reversed.

text_narrative: Gangers on the northern district used to say a manhole could be read from the smell of the benching, and Trewin was the man they meant by it. He laid his benching to a steeper fall than the book asked, cement floated smooth, no ledge anywhere for a rag to catch. Two of his chambers were opened thirty years on and the invert channels were still bright.
text_nonnarrative: Benching in a manhole is to rise from the lip of the channel to the wall at a fall of not less than one in six. A finish in cement mortar, floated and free of ledges, is required on all benching above the half-round. Steps are permitted only in chambers deeper than four feet. Where two channels meet, the benching between them is to be rounded and not squared.

text_narrative: An inquiry into the flooding of a terrace of six houses turned on a single interceptor trap at the head of the private drain. The rodding eye had been left unstopped and a brick had gone in through it, so the trap held solid while the drain above it charged. Water stood four inches in the lowest yard. The surveyor found the seal itself sound and the fault entirely in the missing stopper.
text_nonnarrative: Blockage at an interceptor trap is classed by where the obstruction lies and not by the depth of water standing in the yard. An obstruction in the trap itself, below the seal, is one class; one lodged at the rodding eye, whether brick or rag, is a second, and an unstopped eye is the usual cause of the second and no part of its definition. A sound seal is neutral between the classes.

text_narrative: Each Saturday the cycling club takes the same descent, and each Saturday Ferrig calls the gratings out loud from the front. Two streets down, the bars run with the road and a thin tyre drops between them, so the club swings wide there. Lower, the pattern is crosswise and nobody moves. At the bottom corner one grating sits an inch below its frame and the whole line lifts over it, on the same shout.
text_nonnarrative: Intake at a gully grating is roughly proportional to the open area of the bars, and inversely to the depth of flow over the crown for a fixed grade. Doubling the number of bars while keeping the same open area leaves the intake unaltered but halves the largest object admitted. Beyond a slot width of about one inch the relation to safety of narrow tyres no longer holds in either direction.

text_narrative: In a town where every yard had its midden, there was one scavenger who could name a household from a shovelful, and the council gave him a coat for it. He sorted ash from cinder and cinder from bone and would not mix them, and the heaps he left stood in three colours. When he died the heaps were mixed again in a week, and the town never got its three colours back.
text_nonnarrative: Most writing on midden classification is really writing about respectability. What is called a system in it is usually a list of what the better yards do not keep, so ash and cinder are separated with great care and the interesting residues are lumped as refuse. The accounts worth reading are the ones that count by weight rather than by kind, and there are few of them. The rest are inventories with a moral attached.

text_narrative: Monday, and the copper is on before light, which is the only part of it Sarnet does not mind. Six households, one boiler, and the grate never draws until the flue warms. The sheets will want the second water and the coloureds the third, and by then the fire will be past its best. It is not the boiling that is long. It is the waiting for a copper somebody else has filled.
text_nonnarrative: Shared coppers were reported more often in the older courts than in the newer streets, and the difference was larger between districts than within them. Household size accounted for less of the variation in washing days than the number of families to a boiler. The median wait for a copper, where one was shared by six households, was put at rather over two hours. Coal use per wash varied least of the quantities returned.

text_narrative: The dolly tub stood on two bricks in the scullery and the posser hung on a nail above it, and Odell took it down with both hands because of the weight of the copper cone. Three plunges and a quarter turn, then three more, the way her grandmother had counted. The water went grey at the eighth turn. She rested the handle against the rim and pressed the sheet down with her knuckles instead.
text_nonnarrative: Only the smallest of the four tub sizes was made in staved oak; the rest were galvanised, of twenty, twenty-four and thirty inches across the mouth. Possers were of two patterns, the copper cone pierced with a ring of holes at the shoulder and the plain wooden dolly with three or four legs. The cone was the heavier and was sold with an ash handle of four feet. Ribbed boards were a separate line.

text_narrative: Twice a week the green behind the tenement belongs to one stair, and Halloran keeps the book. On the Tuesday the top stair hangs out and the ropes are up by seven. On the Thursday the ground stair has it and the ropes go up late, because the wash-house is theirs the same morning. On a wet Thursday nobody claims a day back, and Halloran rules the line through anyway.
text_nonnarrative: No claim to the green lay outside a stair's own two days, and a day lost to rain was not recoverable. A rope left up beyond the allotted evening was a trespass on the next stair, whatever the state of the wash. Two stairs could not hold the green together, and an exchange between them was valid only if entered in the book. Initialling was not itself an entry.

text_narrative: Long after the bathhouses were carried out to the stations, the old measure went with them: one cubicle, one hour, and a bell at the half. The founders of the ring held that water carried up a well of that depth was owed more reverence than water drawn from a river, and they wrote the hour into the plate above every door. Later keepers cut it to forty minutes and the plates were left uncut.
text_nonnarrative: A turn, in the regulations of a public bath, meant the period between the opening of a cubicle to one bather and its opening to the next, inclusive of cleansing. Where a bath was let by the hour, the turn was the hour and the cleansing fell within it. Nothing in the schedule of charges affected the length of a turn. A cubicle held open and unlet counted as part of no turn at all.

text_narrative: In the sixth season of the new swimming bath the inlet diffusers were altered, and the minute of that autumn recorded the reason. Cold water had entered in a single stream at the shallow end and lay along the floor as far as the middle rope. Four bronze roses were fitted in place of the two open mouths and the feed was split between the ends. The temperature books were unremarkable.
