text_nonnarrative: Along the shallow end of a covered bath the inlets sit low in the tile, four to a side, a foot above the floor line. The deep end is inletless; its outlets are at the corners. Water is warmest in the middle third and coolest against the shallow wall where the roses are nearest. The gallery above is on the long side only, and the plant is behind the deep end.

text_narrative: A king who had never dug anything ordered his water brought in pipes laid a hand under the turf, because a hand was the depth of his own reach. The first winter split every length of it from the gate to the kitchen court. An old woman of the fen villages was paid a sack of meal to say how deep, and she said three feet and a stone above, and it was done and it held.
text_nonnarrative: Depth of cover for a service pipe was settled less by frost than by traffic, whatever the older manuals said. Frost in most lowland ground was spent within eighteen inches, so two feet would have answered; three feet was the common figure because carts and later paving demanded it. The frost argument was not wrong, but it was doing little work, and where it was the sole ground given the figures were the shallowest.

text_narrative: Anyone who has carried a theodolite over that pass knows the head house at the spring, and knows to sleep outside it. The chamber below the floor is open to the eye and the water comes up clear through gravel, but the roof leaks onto the surface of it and the party that drinks from the chamber tastes the slate. Guides fill from the overflow pipe outside the wall and say nothing about it in camp.
text_nonnarrative: A spring chamber was classed as protected or unprotected on the roof and the floor alone, and the taste of the water was not among the criteria. A chamber open to the surface above was unprotected whatever the gravel below it. A sound roof with an unsealed overflow pipe was a second and lesser class, defective in one particular. The head house wall bore on neither class, being a shelter and not a covering.

text_narrative: A maintenance bulletin from an orbital settlement describes a loss of delivery on the long rising main to the upper farm. Two automatic air valves at the summit of the run are found seized in the closed position, and a pocket of gas stands in the crown for eleven metres. Delivery falls to a third. The valves are replaced with a double-orifice pattern and the summit is fitted with a sight glass.
text_nonnarrative: The head lost to an air pocket is equal to the height of the pocket at the crown, whatever its length along the main, so a long flat summit is worse than a short sharp one only in how much gas it will hold. Orifice area needed at a summit goes with the volume of gas expected and not with the bore of the main. Under a tenth of an atmosphere the accumulation is negligible.

text_narrative: The mangle in the corner of the wash-house has four rollers where every other mangle in the parish has two, and Bettoni has stopped explaining it. Somebody's grandfather put the extra pair in and the sheets come out drier than they should, drier than the weight on the screw accounts for. There is no sense looking underneath. Whatever is under the frame has been under it since before the roof was slated.
text_nonnarrative: Between the frame and the tension screw of a box mangle stood two rollers, each in bearings that were free to rise. The upper roller was the driven one; the lower turned only by contact. The weight lay in a loaded box above and not in the screw, which was a stop rather than a source. Small domestic patterns had no box, and in those the screw carried the whole of the pressure.

text_narrative: There were four penstocks in the wall of the service reservoir and only three keys in the parish, and the fourth spindle turned for nobody. A tinker offered to cut a key for it and was given bread and a bed for the night. In the morning the fourth penstock stood open a quarter and the tinker was gone, and the reservoir ran a hand lower every year after that.
text_nonnarrative: Wedge penstocks are not among the four patterns held in the district store. What is kept there is the plain flap, the rising spindle in two bores, and the non-rising spindle, which is the dearest and the only one with a bronze nut in the headstock. Keys are of one pattern across all three spindle types. Frames come in cast iron only, with a machined seat on the wall face.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the occupation the flushing tanks on the low sewers were emptied by hand, the automatic siphons having been stripped of their bells for the metal. The register for that quarter listed nine tanks so treated and two left charged. Men of the works department carried the water in cans down the ladders twice a week. The bells were recast in the spring from a melted railing.
text_nonnarrative: Automatic flushing tanks were over-praised in the engineering literature of the period. What was called self-acting in them was in truth clock-work of a hydraulic kind, dependent on a steady trickle that few branch supplies could hold; the best of the writing on them admitted as much and treated the siphon as a convenience rather than a cure for flat gradients. The rest was catalogue matter with diagrams.

text_narrative: The old builders held that ground water was owed a road home, and where they could not give it a channel they gave it a pit of stones. Under the floor of every hall of that country lay a shaft filled with rubble, unmortared, so that rain shed from the roof went down into the hill and no wall stood in wet. The last of these builders was buried above one and asked to be.
text_nonnarrative: Calling a soakaway a drain is either a loose usage or a claim about function, and the two are worth keeping apart. A drain in the strict sense is a conductor: it has a destination outside the ground it serves. A soakaway has none, and its capacity is a property of the surrounding soil rather than of the work itself. On the strict usage a soakaway is a store, and storage is not conveyance.
